entries.title: Parsley, Sage, Rosemary, and Ree
entries.summary: “Flesh mixed with gowns, like kneaded satin; that is the substance of flowers.” The line comes from The Voice of Things (1942), a book of prose poems by Francis Ponge in which he muses on the beauty of the commonplace—the erratic flight of butterflies, the pleasure of opening and closing doors—eager to see past an […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
“Flesh mixed with gowns, like kneaded satin; that is the substance of flowers.” The line comes from The Voice of Things (1942), a book of prose poems by Francis Ponge in which he muses on the beauty of the commonplace—the erratic flight of butterflies, the pleasure of opening and closing doors—eager to see past an object’s functional existence into a life beyond.

The artist Rosemary Mayer was drawn to the idea of setting one’s sights on this rich existence of the ordinary material world. She once used Ponge’s line to characterize her sculpture Proserpina (1975), named for the Roman goddess of springtime whose return from the underworld at the end of each winter revived the earth’s flora. This cycle could be seen, Mayer wrote, in the “layered sleeves and robes of historical women’s clothing, recurring spirals, rising and descending.” In Proserpina, eleven vertical yellow wooden rods, enrobed in layers of gray and maroon wire netting, increase in length around a wire-mesh spiral that reaches three feet at its tallest point. Read counterclockwise, the entire structure suggests ascension; read clockwise, it descends.

Proserpina is one of two centerpieces of a small yet effective pairing of rarely seen work by Mayer and Ree Morton from the 1970s and early 1980s at the gallery Gordon Robichaux. Mayer and Morton, who met in New York in the 1970s and were friends, shared an affinity for incorporating fabrics, flowers, and language into work that celebrated women and linked personal history to public display. Morton took inspiration from Neltje Blanchan’s 1917 illustrated book Wild Flowers Worth Knowing, a copy of which is on view alongside a handwritten list of tropical plants that Mayer made around 1975. The visual potential of some of the entries from the two documents—“firewheel tree,” “toadflax,” and “heal-all”—is borne out in the artists’ work.

The other centerpiece of the show is Morton’s sculpture Devil Chaser, made the same year as Proserpina. “Devil chaser” is another name for Saint-John’s-wort, a flowering herb used in medicinal remedies. In the nearly four-foot-long work, a plantlike cage is attached to what might be a ground snare or a captured devil’s tail. Snippets from Blanchan’s commentary about the plant appear on nearby plaques: “TO REVEAL THE PRESENCE OF WITCHES,” “TO WARD OFF DESTRUCTION BY LIGHTNING,” “TO CURE DEMONIACS.”

In 1974 Morton discovered Celastic, a material widely used in the theater industry that acts like fabric but cures to a rigid form. For Devil Chaser, she wrapped the wire armature in Celastic and painted it a mottled peachy pink. She then embellished the cage-like end with Celastic ribbons in bright colors. Red coils dangle playfully from the loop at the other end—perhaps exotic blooms, devilish tendrils, or attractive bait. Set on a rectangle of green, Devil Chaser was, in its original form, bordered by an undulating decorative fence, giving it the appearance of a tidy garden or a place of protection. (These sections of fence have been distributed around the perimeter of the room in order to “expand” the garden, though their purpose and effect are diminished.)

The show also includes thirteen drawings and paintings by the two artists. Mayer’s watercolors AS SAFE AS HOUSES, HARMLESS DAYS, and NOW WITH A WHOLE SKIN, all from 1983, join tender renderings of flowers with idioms related to safety, a sentiment that rhymes with Devil Chaser. The petaled flower heads in Mayer’s exquisite watercolor Date Column (1976) have the look of gathered fabric—an effect echoed in Morton’s cheerful Celastic bows, or Beaux (circa 1974), as she titled them, two of which ornament opposite walls. Hung around the gallery like signposts are word paintings from Morton’s celebratory installation Signs of Love (1976). “Gestures,” “Settings,” “Atmospheres”—the words are redolent of art making, gardens, and life.

Another major element at play in the show is friendship. In 1975 Morton created the installation Something in the Wind, comprising more than a hundred hand-sewn and painted flags, each dedicated to a family member, friend, or artist, inspired by a book Mayer loaned her about coats of arms. For the installation, she raised the flags on the rigging of a ship at the South Street Seaport. The flag representing Mayer bears a butterfly and stitched letters spelling out “ROSEMARY.” On April 30, 1977, Morton died in a car crash. Mayer wrote to a friend about her difficulty processing Morton’s death, deciding that “Ree floats in instead,” suggesting that the loss and her feelings about it would always be airy, elusive things. The next year she made Some Days in April, a “temporary monument” in which she wrote the names of deceased friends and family on balloons. Near Morton’s flag in the show hangs Mayer’s Some Days in April (Helen) (1978), a drawing of the balloon she’d made for Morton. It displays Morton’s given name, Helen; Mayer’s chosen name, Catherine; and the words “Arcturus” and “Narcissus,” a star and a flower that reappear each spring.

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In any story by the Scottish writer Ali Smith, you are likely to find a precocious young person who delivers a dose of naked truth, exposing the shams of contemporary mores and politics. You may also find a ghost. These figures often serve as catalysts. They shake other characters awake and chivy them along toward whatever small changes or revelations are possible within the scope of the story. They can be main characters, like the young narrator of Smith’s recent novel Gliff (2024), but more often they turn up unexpectedly, introducing a little wobble in the ongoing narrative, a shade of doubt.

Smith’s ghosts can be driven by the needs of their new, changed condition, as in her second novel, Hotel World (2001), or as transient and unassuming as the floating head of a Victorian child that visits an isolated woman in Winter (2017), a Dickensian touch for a Christmas novel. A ghost may resemble the human it once was, but not wholly. The afterlife strips something from us.

When a dead lover returns in Artful (2012), Smith’s collection of her four semifictional Weidenfeld lectures, she can barely speak or think. She is covered in debris, as if she’d been dropped through the walls of an old house, gathering the detritus of years. The lecture she appears in is called “On Time,” and like other Smith specters, she’s as much a manifestation of the past itself as of a specific person. The bereaved narrator accepts that this weird, grimy version of her lost love is not “real” as we typically understand the term:

I had to congratulate my imagination, for you were very like you. Though I’d never have imagined the imagination could be so good with smell; you smelt quite strong for something or someone imaginary. Either way, you’d come back, and it was about time.

Smith’s ghosts are rarely gloomy—or only intermittently. Death, where is thy sting if we get to hang around incorporeally for a while? They provide the ultimate narrative pivot: Surprise! Still here! And Smith offsets their metaphoric gravitas—their associations with loss, separation, and the riptide of time—with the comic potential of scaring the living or offering pert, disembodied opinions on art. Her ghosts reach back to folklore, but they are also creatures of our dark and boggy present, of our anxieties and disconnection. “I’ve a feeling I’ve inherited them from whatever Scottish literary family I belong to,” she said on the Canadian radio show Bookends.

Smith’s recent paired novels Gliff and Glyph (2026) both feature precocious young siblings. Glyph also has ghosts—and of a type new to Smith’s fiction. One human, one equine, they form what we might call “story ghosts,” the afterimages of powerful stories we can’t process or forget. They haunt as effectively as any jilted bride.

In Gliff, a dystopian novel set in a near-future Britain, two middle-school-aged children, Rose and Briar (Bri), are separated from their mother under mysterious circumstances and abandoned by their mother’s boyfriend, Leif, who may or may not have stolen their passports to sell. The family has been chased from its home by some government body that paints ominous red lines around buildings, cars, and people. Red-lined buildings are slated for demolition and redevelopment; “unverifiable” folk get carted off for reeducation. The hint to move on is unmissable.

In a last act of kindness, Leif brings the siblings to a new town and finds them a stripped nineteenth-century railway worker’s cottage to squat in until his promised return. From this home base, the older sibling, Bri—whose gender is never specified in the novel and who prefers not to be labeled—explores the town, while Rose discovers a group of horses, destined for the knacker, in a field nearby. She befriends a gray gelding and, having learned what the term “abattoir” means, convinces Bri to buy the horse with the last of their money. Rose names him Gliff, since she’d been warned the horse was “gliffy”—hard to handle. This magnificent creature must be concealed but cannot live inside their house for long. For help, they seek out other unverifiable people living secretly at a boarded-up school in town and discover there, among other wonders, a large library and some outmoded but functional computers.

Rose and Bri’s mother, an environmental whistleblower who lives almost as a fugitive, has kept her children away from new technologies and out of the public record. She considers smartphones a liability, not only because they can be tracked—state surveillance is a constant danger in Gliff—but because once you have one, “you see everything through it.” She would prefer her children to learn from the real world. She homeschooled them with her few books; as a result, the siblings share an uncommon knowledge of herbal healing.

Yet Bri is effortlessly “good with machines and tech.” Whenever they get near a laptop they revel in looking up words: “It was always exciting to me the number of things a single word could mean.” Online, then in the school library, they look up “gliff” and find almost two pages of definitions—an incantatory list (both real and fictional) that includes “to glimpse,” “to frighten,” and “to strike a glancing blow at someone or something.” They also try to decipher the Latin motto on the front of the school—Facta sunt ipse verba—marveling that

there was such a thing as a family of words, one that stretched across different languages all touching on each other, hitting or striking each other, acting on each other, influencing each other, agreeing with each other or throwing each other out, disturbing each other, doing all of these things at once.

Bri’s rapture recalls Virginia Woolf’s 1937 essay “Craftmanship,” a small section of which, taped for the BBC, constitutes the only surviving recording of her plummy Edwardian voice. (Its centering diphthongs, a feature now confined to a few well-heeled nonagenarians, make “survive” verge on three syllables.) Words, Woolf wrote in that essay, “are the wildest, freest, most irresponsible, most unteachable of all things.” The difficulty in modern writing, she argued, is that old words are “so stored with meanings, with memories” that they are hard to combine with new words: they have already “contracted so many famous marriages.”

Smith’s characters frequently swoon over dictionaries, but Woolf would have disapproved: “Words do not live in dictionaries; they live in the mind.” She resented the constraints (and exclusions) of the great institutions and their codifiers. Her father edited the Dictionary of National Biography and was an early reader for the Oxford English Dictionary: one reason why, to Woolf, a dictionary was a patriarchal rule book—and not even a complete or impartial one.1

In compiling The Book Lover (2006), a collection of excerpts from some of her favorite and formative reading, Smith realized so many came from Woolf that “maybe this would have to be a Woolf anthology.” Aside from their feminism and stylistic affinities, they both write in service of books, libraries, and the freedom to read. Even Smith’s metaphors are often based on books and language; when a teenager, Magnus, falls in love with a charismatic interloper in her novel The Accidental (2005), he feels “she had entered him like he was water. Like he was a dictionary and she was a word he hadn’t known was in him.”

Smith loves to consider etymologies and their cultural implications. Almost all her novels include etymologies, which she uses as pivots—a way in, a way out, a thematic expansion—and as washes of unexpected color. In a 2025 interview with NPR, she was asked about an early job writing advertising copy for her brother’s business. Her memories of a biscuit jingle she came up with spark a meditation on the word “slogan”:

It’s connected to the English word slughorn, because it comes from a Gaelic word that sounds more like sluggern. And sluggern and slughorn meant a war cry. So slogans are directly descended from warfare and war cries—the noise that one tribe makes when it’s facing another and it blows its horn going [imitating horn blowing]. Buy Paterson Bronte Golden Crunch, the perfect fireside snack [imitating horn blowing]. Almost everything about slogans can be connected to the tribal in us, which is why they work so well.2

In Gliff it is hard not to see her brainy youths as self-portraits, especially when Bri rushes to share their list of definitions for “gliff” with Rose: “See, listen, you’ve actually called him something unpindownable. Something really excitingly polysemous…. Polysemous. I looked that word up too.” Not only Smith’s formal experiments but her constant wordplay, punning, and riffing give her prose a sense of superabundance, of endless, rapid-fire invention held back—sometimes belatedly—by her perception that she has taken her reader too far into the ether. Smith wrote her doctoral dissertation on the ordinary in modernist literature, so the balance between what Woolf called “granite and rainbow” (the solidity of “truth” or material reality and the insubstantial qualities of personality or emotion) has long been on her mind.3

Smith was born in Inverness in 1962, the youngest (by six years) of five children in a working-class family. Her father was an electrician and contractor with a gift for storytelling, and her mother helped in his shop. Neither parent was able to complete school, but they prized education for their children. The Smiths had only two artworks in the house, one a well-known print of bluebell woods that her mother could not resist and that her father thought a waste of money. When Smith evokes her mother’s ghost in a recent art catalog for the Munch Museum, So in the Spruce Forest (2025), she gives her a penetrating critical sensibility, restoring an art education she had never had:

Then the voice from nowhere carried on talking about Munch, like my mother of all people knew about Munch, like she knew I was looking at a picture right now, like she knew about the power crisis and the international unrest and the climate ruination in a world she’d left thirty years ago. Like she knew it all.

It was lovely to hear her voice again.

As a child Smith read her siblings’ schoolbooks and later realized she had absorbed much of the canon (Joyce, Orwell, Swift) before the age of ten. Almost as important were the two cinemas in town, one of which showed foreign films on weekends. When Smith digresses in her fiction, she often writes about representation, about how stories and films work; near the middle of The Accidental is a two-page tour de force on cinema, a floating first-person account of the filmic formation of some collective, unnamed narrator whose experiences are shared almost universally. “My mother was a nun who could no longer stand the convent,” we learn.

She married my father, the captain; he was very strict. She taught us all to sing and made us new clothes out of curtains….

When I was a child I ran the Grand National on my horse. They didn’t know I was a girl until I fainted and they unbuttoned my jockey shirt.

Glyph, for its part, pulls in many of the narrative beats from Laurel and Hardy’s Wrong Again (1929), in which the hapless duo brings a horse inside.

Smith studied English at the University of Aberdeen and went on to Newnham College, Cambridge, for a Ph.D. There she met her future partner, Sarah Wood—a filmmaker and artist and Smith’s frequent collaborator—when Wood directed a play of hers. Smith taught English and American literature for eighteen months at the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow, but she felt alienated by the changes occurring in academia, including the recasting of universities as businesses. She developed chronic fatigue syndrome at twenty-seven and took months to recover. As she later put it, “I had to stop so that I could decide which road to cross.” She returned to Cambridge, where she wrote the stories in her first book, Free Love and Other Stories (1995), which won the Saltire First Book of the Year Award.

Her debut novel, Like, followed two years later. Like’s autobiographical elements include aspects of the class divide and the unequal relationship between Scotland and England. Smith introduces some of the doubling and layering that build in her later work. Timelines weave. Fire is a recurrent theme; one of the main characters goes by Ash, short for Aisling. In retrospect, the novel is also about the closet, about the displacement and destruction that result when two girls can’t just love each other.

Four of Smith’s novels have been short-listed for the Booker, but her most celebrated book is probably How to Be Both (2014), her sixth novel, composed of two separate but interconnected narratives set five hundred years apart. It was published in two versions, each beginning with one of those narratives. (Smith’s publisher split the print run in half; the covers were identical.) One part of How to Be Both features a dead narrator, the Quattrocento painter Francesco del Cossa (secretly a cross-dressing girl in this novel), who finds himself “shot back into being like an arrow [to] find myself now in this intermediate place.” Cossa really existed but left almost no biographical record—a perfect opportunity to invent one. The other part is a contemporary story in which a woman drags her adolescent daughter to Ferrara to see the enchanting frescoes Cossa painted with Cosmè Tura at the Palazzo Schifanoia (the Palace of Escape from Boredom).

Smith’s work takes a darker turn after How to Be Both, reflecting the political turmoil of the past ten years, especially the refugee crisis, climate change, and new legal restrictions on free expression and street protest. Her seasonal quartet, which begins with Autumn (2016) and ends with Summer (2020), is both a love letter to nature and art and a counterpunch to the rise of the far right.4 She intended the quartet to be about longevity, she said in an interview with The Paris Review, “and, at the same time, about the surface of whatever was happening in the world at the time the book was being written.”

They do function as state-of-Britain novels, though their sociopolitical concerns will feel familiar across the globe. Also familiar are the stupid bureaucratic snarls that arise from tighter regulations (at the bank, at the post office, at the passport bureau), the sense of everything getting worse and harder, and of our collective exhaustion at constant loss, shock, and forced adjustment. When a character in Spring (2019) visits his dying friend, he asks, “How’re you doing, apart from the end of liberal capitalist democracy?” Spring could serve as a sister novel to Gliff, with its gifted young person—this one a bit magical, to suit the season—and its underground network of rescuers, its stubborn assertion that kindness can still change the world.

Gliff, which won the 2026 Dublin Literary Award, began as a short story commissioned for an anthology of Kafka-inspired fiction, A Cage Went in Search of a Bird (2024). That story, “Art Hotel,” unseated the novel Smith had been working on and, lightly edited, became the opening chapters of Gliff. The bureaucratic menace of Kafka’s 1925 The Trial looms over the unverifiables of the novel, but its presiding spirit is Orwell, who would recognize the double life Bri constructs as the plot develops: a sliver of authenticity and remembered happiness sealed off from their outward conformity to an authoritarian system. In that hidden self lies Bri’s tenacious bond with Rose, long after circumstances drive Rose and Gliff away from her.

It sounds flip to describe Gliff as Smith’s glyphosate novel, but her wordplay in the homophone titles Gliff and Glyph is intentional. In between the publications of the two novels, the UK license for glyphosate, the chemical used in herbicides like Roundup, was extended until mid-December 2026, although its toxicity and environmental dangers are well documented.5 While pregnant with Rose, Bri’s mother had written public relations copy for the weed killer conglomerate Kindweed, trying to convince buyers of its safety. She tells Bri that a former employee, a chemist, confided that the weed killer “didn’t just poison weeds and grasses and flowers and insects, but was also unsafe for lots of other bigger living things. Including dogs, and birds, and cows, and the milk that came from them.” And horses, we assume, as well as humans, especially children and developing fetuses. The product marketed as Kindweed’s gentlest is secretly the same as the company’s most virulent. When Bri’s mother began quietly asking questions, she was sacked.

The relationship between Gliff and Glyph is like a set of mirrors installed at irregular angles, the last of which reflects something outside. Themes are repeated, including the sibling bond. Other correspondences flash and fade. The news is ominous and true to life—AI takeover, economic collapse—but Glyph has a tonal shift, a puckish quality that feels more characteristic of Smith’s earlier fiction than Gliff does. The plot centers on two middle-aged sisters, Petra and Patricia (“Patch”) Wild, who have barely spoken after the bruising experience of sorting their dead parents’ possessions eight years earlier. They shared a tense childhood; after their loving mother died young, their father, prone to outbursts, withdrew into angry silence when not punishing Petra, the elder of the two. A few pages into Glyph, we learn that Gliff is a speculative dystopian novel that Patch has sent Petra as an olive branch. Patch’s foster daughter, Billie, had been reading it, “phone usually glued to the hand but for three whole days it was nothing but a book.”

What really caught Patch’s eye was the title. When the sisters were young, not long before their mother died, Petra invented a ghost—or rather, pretended to contact one in order to comfort Patch. The girls had heard a real-life horror story from World War II about a corpse found flattened on a road in France, as if run over and over by a convoy of tanks, and Patch couldn’t sleep afterward. Petra pretends to ring up the flattened man, who is fine in the afterlife: “He said that he doesn’t really like being reminded of what happened to him but that you thinking of him had made him very moved and pleased.” They were both, Petra suggests, “to go to sleep now and wake up tomorrow free from worry.” Patch believes and disbelieves in this phone call with the dead. But the ghost, instead of remaining a onetime “jeu d’esprit,” as Petra’s worried mother calls him, sticks around, becoming real enough to name. They call him “Glyph.”

Once Gliff stirs the memory of their ghost, Petra feels a surge of guilt, the clear

wrongness in what we were doing, using a terrible true story, the ghost or the shade of a story, about something abysmal that I’m assuming really did happen to someone real, to distract ourselves from feeling what we must no doubt have been feeling, and sensing, round what turned out to be—and look at me now even in this sentence still keeping it at a distance—our mother’s impending death.

As the only redress she can imagine, she launches an extensive online search to try to find anything “real and true” about the dead man. But her thoughts are interrupted by bouts of clattering noise in her house, as if her neighbor were throwing furniture. And what is that smell? She finally throws open a door to find a spectral horse tearing apart her bedroom. Petra’s first call is to Patch, to lay a ghost (or two) to rest and try to mend their estrangement.

The wartime story at the heart of Glyph originates with the writer Xandra Bingley, Smith’s former agent. A member of Bingley’s family had encountered the flattened corpse on a road in the south of France near the end of the war. “Someone tells you something and it goes into you like osmosis,” Smith told an interviewer on the BBC radio show Take Four Books. “And I have not been able to stop thinking about this for a long time.” She had the story in mind while writing Gliff, but she “couldn’t actually face it. I couldn’t get near it. I couldn’t get to the kind of horrific quality of the removal of dimension from the human being. I couldn’t get near it until…I’d written the first book.”

In Glyph, Petra watches what seems like Gaza coverage on television while completing a Duolingo lesson on her phone. Increasingly, in Smith’s work, technology has been tied to the question of witnessing and to our increasing numbness to suffering. A character in Winter realizes she “had been feeling nothing for some time now. Refugees in the sea. Children in ambulances. Blood-soaked men running to hospitals or away from burning hospitals carrying blood-covered children.” In How to Be Both, a teenager is traumatized by accidentally clicking on a website displaying a child rape. She vows never to turn away from abuse, never to choose anesthesia.

In Regarding the Pain of Others (2003), Susan Sontag argued that visual depictions of suffering could diminish lived experience and risked becoming mere aesthetic objects, especially if displayed in a gallery or museum. Private viewing might preserve the emotional effect, she thought. She could not have foretold the bovine trance in which we scroll past hundreds of images a day on our own tiny screens.

Many of Smith’s novels have addressed the rise of consumer technologies. As early as There but for the (2011), she brilliantly described Google search as a “whole new way of feeling lonely,” with its

semblance of plenitude but really a new level of Dante’s inferno, a zombie-filled cemetery of spurious clues, beauty, pathos, pain, the faces of puppies, women and men from all over the world tied up and wanked over in site after site, a great sea of hidden shallows.

Terrible things also happen to books in Smith’s work. For a writer so fiercely supportive of public libraries and so dreamily susceptible to what the diarist W.N.P. Barbellion called the “almost audible susurrus of desire—the desire every book has to be taken down and read,” Smith seems to enjoy mangling them. One character in an early story tears out the pages of her books one by one as she finishes reading them. Like ends with a shocking conflagration, though books are punished throughout, perhaps made to bear their young writer’s anxieties of authorship. Or it may be that familiarity does breed contempt—or at least overwhelm, as those with book heaps can attest. At a bookstore event to promote So in the Spruce Forest, Wood and Smith described leaving a book outside to see how the elements worked on it.6 They think it was The Tempest.

Smith is gentler to books in Gliff and Glyph, however, as if they are friends down on their luck. In Glyph, a book reconnects estranged siblings—a reminder of a shared literary culture we used to idealize (like a tidal island, not always reachable from the mainland). And in Gliff, with its wondrously preserved school library, we revisit the mind-expanding potential of books, the radical freedom they embody as freedom recedes elsewhere: “Wherever my eye went, books. Oh! I said.”

entries.title: Let a Hundred Websites Bloom
entries.summary: The Internet and the smartphone have become formidable tools for the Chinese government to maintain tight control over society.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
When I arrived in Shanghai in the early 2000s to begin a half-decade assignment covering China, I often marveled at the distance between the common Western image of the country as a repressive dictatorship and the many spaces for communication that seemed to escape the government’s control. My first inklings of this came in random encounters with Chinese people, in bank lines, on trains, or on the sidelines of public events. They were as curious about the world that had produced me as I was about the world that had produced them. Moreover, many seemed as disinclined to pull punches in expressing criticism of their society as I was of mine.

These early impressions quickly deepened as I began to explore the country’s Internet. Certainly there were clear taboos, beginning with questioning the legitimacy of the Chinese Communist Party and criticizing the country’s central leadership. Alongside these topics were the forbidden so-called big Ts: Tibet, Taiwan, and Tiananmen. But surprisingly large realms of online speech remained wide open. Without too much effort, one could find public threads about almost anything else. And people used bulletin boards and discussion groups on Chinese Web platforms like Weibo and QQ to report official malfeasance or corruption at the local or regional level.

During my first years in China, much of my time was spent covering localized protests that gathered strength online. Municipal and provincial officials worked tirelessly to suppress the amplification of whistleblowing and dissent, but the surge in accountability activism and citizen journalism that the early Internet brought to the country reduced their efforts to a futile game of whack-a-mole. Often all that Web-based activists needed to do to evade sanction during local crackdowns was to temporarily set themselves up in a nearby province.

A similar laxity existed about online name verification. Back then there were few practical obstacles to using assumed names on the Web. Those who sought an extra layer of personal security while commenting on risky topics conducted their online life from the grimy and smoke-filled confines of the era’s ubiquitous Internet cafés, where they periodically changed their aliases. Others frequently replaced the SIM cards in their phones.

Once in a while, what began as a very local event would suddenly mushroom into a national outcry over some injustice that hinted at the surviving, if atrophied, democratic potential of a population living under a self-proclaimed dictatorship of the proletariat. That was the case in 2003, the year of my arrival in China, when a twenty-seven-year-old migrant laborer, Sun Zhigang, was arrested in Guangzhou for not carrying proper identification papers and then was beaten to death in detention. The case was heavily covered by the seemingly fearless Southern Metropolis Daily, a muckraking newspaper. But news about it soon spread much farther via the Internet and sparked outrage in viral posts and discussion groups. Almost astoundingly in a country known for strict, top-down control, three months after Sun was killed, the central government dismantled the heavy-handed and secretive national custody system used to detain Chinese workers who violated the country’s strict residential permit system.

In March 2000 Bill Clinton had come close to predicting that the advent of the Web would bring about a radical relaxation of top-down political control in China: “Now, there’s no question China has been trying to crack down on the Internet—good luck. That’s sort of like trying to nail jello to the wall.” Although I wasn’t betting against the possibility that censorship would win out in the long run in China, during my early years there one could still imagine that Clinton might have been right. But that is no longer the case.

Since I left the country, the entire landscape of online life and the political space enjoyed by its citizens have shrunk radically. This has happened in part because of the ubiquitous rise of the smartphone, which has proven to be the perfect tool for state surveillance, censorship, and much more strictly enforced conformity. There are many reasons for this, beginning with the fact that China belatedly began enforcing the requirement to show official identification in order to get SIM cards, which made aliases useless and eliminated the protection of anonymity. What is worse, smartphones make it easy for the state to document their owners’ every movement and communication.

Easily as important as these features, though, has been the astonishingly fast and nearly universal adoption of China’s powerful homegrown app, WeChat, which has established itself as a one-stop clearinghouse for almost everything that non-Chinese smartphone users accomplish with a plethora of apps. In China, people not only chat through WeChat, they also use it as a social media platform, rely on it for news and entertainment, and use it to bank, shop, make travel arrangements, conduct their business, and even pay taxes and government fines. WeChat’s astonishing rise took place not long after I left China in 2008, and its hold on the society is so pervasive that for any outsider like me who wishes to stay in touch with friends there or to navigate the country during visits, maintaining an account and mastering its functions are essential.

The other development of enormous consequence for freedom of speech and the degree of openness in China, of course, has been the ascension of the country’s current leader, Xi Jinping. Since he became president in 2013, the ruling Communist Party has placed an emphasis on social control unseen in China at least since Mao Zedong’s heyday. Mao relied on neighborhood committees to surveil behavior down to the street level and often encouraged family members to inform on one another. But Xi enjoys powers of real-time monitoring that Mao could have never dreamed of.

Xi has also doubled or even tripled down on the once-leaky online censorship system known colloquially as the Great Firewall, which not only polices domestic online communications but is also a powerful filter of information from the outside world. I can’t forget my surprise at glimpsing some of the crude inner workings of the early Great Firewall. When I visited a university in Shanghai in 2006, students ushered me into a control room where dozens of campus volunteers were monitoring the online communications of their peers. After my visit, the university’s party secretary told me sheepishly that this wasn’t something the authorities were interested in advertising.

Nowadays, although armies of Web censors are not altogether obsolete, they take a distant backseat to highly sophisticated automated monitoring and surveillance systems, and every Chinese person I’ve ever known is aware of this and assumes its effectiveness, which deters risky speech. As a result, rather than facilitating political change in China, the Internet and the associated world of the mobile phone have become formidable tools the government uses to maintain tight control over the society.

Yi-Ling Liu came of age just as this tide was shifting. After being raised in Hong Kong, then still a wide-open global city where near-Western levels of personal liberties and the rule of law largely prevailed, she went to Beijing in 2010 to work as an intern for a Chinese media company. Learning about the 1989 Tiananmen massacre as a high school student had fed her interest in China’s history, including in recurrent attempts by both ordinary Chinese citizens and political insiders to spark national reform. After graduating from Yale, she writes in The Wall Dancers: Searching for Freedom and Connection on the Chinese Internet,

I returned to Beijing to live and write, because I still wanted to know—not just what could’ve been changed at the square that day but also what could be changed today and who had the power to do the changing.

Liu’s account differs from most recent writing about China by Western journalists in eschewing assessments of the country based on its elite politics or on insights gleaned from interviews with experts. Western journalists have faced sharply restricted access to China under Xi’s rule. In following the history of Internet activism in China, what Liu offers instead is a bottom-up sense of life and the state of personal freedom in the country. Along the way, something striking happens. Rather than confirming the West’s smugness about its individual liberties and democracy compared to China’s, her book slowly builds to the disquieting conclusion that the crushing power of the Internet is steadily making the United States and China more like each other.

The Wall Dancers serves up any number of milestones—like the Sun Zhigang case—that would be familiar to anyone who has followed the country closely since the 2000s. As she recounts, these culminated in what became known as the Weibo Spring, the name given to a period of extraordinary online activism in 2011 that followed the more familiar Arab Spring of protest and reform movements.

Perhaps the biggest catalyst for that year’s breakout activism was a deadly collision in Wenzhou between one of China’s brand-new bullet trains and another train that was stopped on the same track. The impressively rapid introduction this century of high-speed rail service, by now virtually nationwide, has been a major focus of the government’s nationalist propaganda. The crash officially killed forty people and injured nearly two hundred, making it the world’s third-deadliest high-speed rail collision.

The first post about it on Weibo, which went up almost immediately, was a cry for help by a university student who was a passenger. It was immediately reposted by others, as millions of people turned to the social media platform for a more detailed picture of the crash than the government’s sanitized news offered. What ensued was a dramatic, real-time contest between citizens and censors. The next day the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Propaganda Department issued a terse directive to the country’s media: “Do not question. Do not elaborate. Do not associate.”

This meant that only official accounts of the accident would be allowed to circulate. But citizen skepticism had been boosted by official actions that hinted strongly at a cover-up. These included the prompt burial of the wreckage near the crash site and the failure to publish a list of the victims. The online outcry that followed was so intense that China’s then premier, Wen Jiabao, felt obliged to visit the site and promise a full investigation. “If corruption was found behind this, we must handle it according to law, and we will not be lenient,” he said. Later the railway minister at the time was tried and sentenced to life imprisonment for bribery.

The central government’s inability to suppress citizen grievances that forced an official as high-ranking as Wen to promise justice gave the Wenzhou train crash the feeling of a watershed. For the first time in China, it was becoming possible, it seemed, for citizens to use the Internet to hold their remote and controlling government to account. What the accident seems to have accomplished instead was to make the state even more determined that it would never again be so vulnerable to waves of public outcry spreading online.

Liu’s book distinguishes itself by going far beyond well-known events like this, with rich, extended profiles of individuals who had begun using the Internet to try to build new lives for themselves or to change China during the era when the Internet still seemed to offer the possibility of a freer future. For example, in the late 1990s Ma Baoli, a gay junior policeman in the provincial town of Qinhuangdao, began spending his free time at a new Internet café that had opened near his police station. There he began a process of self-discovery and growing awareness of the existence of large numbers of gay men who, like him, lived in the shadows. He joined online forums like Chinese Men’s and Boy’s Paradise, read online gay fiction, and watched “every gay film he could get his hands on, sobbing over his takeout noodles.”

Using a pseudonym, Ma created a website for gay men, Light Blue Memories. After he primed it with his own stories about unrequited love and loneliness and with melancholy reflections about fleeting youth, it took off. In its early years, Ma was obliged to sustain a guerrilla-style backup operation that could relocate his servers from one municipality to another each time authorities tried to close the website on the grounds of indecency.

As it exploded in popularity, Ma rented space in Beijing, a four-hour train ride from his hometown, and commuted back and forth as he managed his dual identities: police officer and host of a social platform for gay people. In March 2012, though, he made the fateful decision to be featured in a documentary about his website, which prompted a huge and unexpected response. The film was covered positively on the home page of Sohu, one of the country’s biggest news portals. It also prompted an angry summons from his boss, who called Ma’s site humiliating for the police.

Ma resigned from the department the next day and, far from being discouraged, created a dating app for gay men, which he named Blued. It soon rocketed to number nine in downloads from China’s Apple app store. In November 2012 China’s minister of health invited Ma to participate in that year’s World AIDS Day conference in Beijing. There, to his surprise, he found himself face-to-face with Premier Li Keqiang and introduced himself, saying, “Greetings, Premier. I run a gay website.” In a scene that played that night on national television, Li shook his hand without missing a beat and said, “Thank you for your hard work, comrade.”

The story of another of Liu’s characters, Lü Pin, follows a somewhat similar arc. After acquiring a graduate degree in Chinese literature in 1994, she took a job at a stodgy state-run newspaper, China Women’s News. Although she had had little prior interest in women’s issues, Lü underwent a steady awakening and soon found herself chafing at the limits she faced in writing about gender inequality for a quasi-official publication. With her sharpness and drive, she nonetheless rose steadily up the paper’s hierarchy and found herself one step away from the deputy editor’s job at age thirty.

In a decision that shocked friends and colleagues, Lü resigned rather than pursue the promotion. To enter senior management, she would have had to join the Chinese Communist Party, and as someone who identified as part of the “1989 generation”—people who came of age around the time of the Tiananmen demonstrations—this was something she couldn’t do unless the party properly faced up to the history of the massacre there.

Lü then took a job in local government in Gansu, a relatively poor province, where she began writing freelance stories about the condition of women in China. Her goal all along was to reach a general audience, not just specialists and intellectuals, but these stories had a sparse readership. Another national public scandal, however, eventually provided Lü the opportunity to reach many more people.

In May 2009 Deng Yujiao, a twenty-one-year-old waitress in a karaoke club in Hubei province, was cornered in the club’s restroom by two local officials who demanded “special services” from her, meaning sex. When she refused, one of them smacked her in the face with a wad of banknotes, shouting, “Don’t you want money? Would you believe if I am going to beat you to death with money today?” Deng stabbed him in the neck with a fruit knife and called the police as he bled out.

Liu is almost certainly correct when she writes that in the pre-Internet era, this incident would have gotten little attention and Deng would have been convicted of homicide, especially since the victim was an official. Instead it went viral, with citizens expressing outrage over a range of issues, from the hints of official corruption in the wad of cash, to the male presumption of a right to sex, to the imagined impunity of the assailants. Amid a gale of public outcry, the charges were dropped.

That September, fired up by these events, Lü founded Women’s Voices, a digital magazine dedicated to women’s rights. At a reader’s suggestion, she soon changed the name to Feminist Voices. Lü wrote prolifically, her publication quickly gained traction with readers, and it helped spawn a loose but energized movement with headquarters in a two-bedroom apartment in Beijing that she called the One Yuan Commune. Every summer it hosted open courses on feminism to highly receptive attendees. “Our society does not allow for alternative views—be it about gender, sexuality, or politics—and those with different views find themselves isolated, rejected by the mainstream, with nowhere to go,” Lü later wrote.

With wind in its sails, the women’s movement that Lü helped create became bolder. It staged acts of guerrilla theater, such as a Valentine’s Day demonstration by three young women in Qianmen, one of Beijing’s busiest commercial districts. They dressed in cheap wedding gowns for the occasion, smeared their bodices with lipstick to resemble blood, and brushed their faces with eyeshadow to mimic bruising. “Yes to love, no to violence,” they chanted as they marched, in denunciation of domestic violence.

Liu tells the stories of Lü and Ma as a study in diverging approaches to how citizens inclined toward activism can relate to the state: the one accommodating and the other militant. But neither, any more than the Wenzhou crash, was a true harbinger of reform and opening in China.

Starting from his successful gay dating site, Ma Baoli built a queer entertainment empire that produced television shows and partnered with queer NGOs. But these early successes were deceptive, and Ma’s company eventually provoked a strong backlash from the state. After it produced a Web series about love between two high school boys called Addicted in 2016, China’s media regulators announced a ban on all portrayals of what it called “abnormal sexual relations,” including same-sex relations. Since then Ma has meekly complied, surviving, as Liu writes, by “always staying in the government’s good graces.”

Lü’s dark reckoning came even sooner. In March 2015, while she was visiting New York to attend the United Nations Commission on the Status of Women conference, Chinese police mounted a multicity roundup of five of the core members of her movement. Lü sent hundreds of emails to raise an international protest, and Hillary Clinton and Samatha Power were among those who condemned the arrests. The five were released after thirty-seven days in detention, but Feminist Voices was shut down and Lü was effectively forced into exile. The state, in the end, found ways to foreclose both of their efforts to loosen state control on gender and social mores in China from the bottom up.

During the Xi years another era has closed in China: from roughly 2007 until 2019 the appetite of young Chinese for study overseas, and particularly in the United States, seemed insatiable. In that peak final year, 372,000 Chinese were pursuing degrees in American colleges and universities. The outbreak of Covid-19 reduced this number by about 50,000, but since the end of the pandemic it has continued to drop, reaching 266,000 last year.

Jimmy Carter had made human rights a centerpiece of his foreign policy, including the right of citizens of Communist countries to emigrate. When the issue of emigration arose during Deng Xiaoping’s 1979 White House visit, Deng turned the argument on its head. “Would you like to import ten million Chinese?” he asked. “There is no question like that for China.” In fact, for many years afterward, if never remotely on this scale, China sent large numbers of students abroad, basing its hopes of catching up economically with the West on the education and training of rising numbers of its best students in American schools.

China’s modern economic takeoff, which began under Deng, has far outstripped almost all early expectations, including his. But it was long shadowed by often-stated doubts. Western politicians, pundits, and even economists said that a strategy of absorbing knowledge from overseas might enable China to catch up, but they questioned whether the country could ever become a leader in innovation and intellectual output, especially as long as it had a closed political system.

China’s economy has slowed in recent years, but its innovation across a number of domains, from electric vehicles and batteries to industrial robots, artificial intelligence, and space exploration, has finally quieted skeptics. Nowadays the Chinese government no longer encourages its students to study overseas, a reflection of another enormous achievement: the rapid rise of its own universities as worthy rivals of the best the West has to offer. The decline in the numbers of Chinese studying abroad has been further accelerated by increasingly restrictive immigration policies in the United States under Donald Trump.

In The Highest Exam: How the Gaokao Shapes China, Ruixue Jia and Hongbin Li argue that one of the most important factors in China’s resurgence through education has ironically been the modern implementation of the gaokao, its little-known and widely misunderstood ancient scholarly examination system. The gaokao is a grueling standardized test administered nationally to roughly 13 million students over two or four days each summer. Its core subjects are Chinese language and literature, mathematics, and a foreign language, which usually means English. Students also choose between electives of science or the humanities.

Whereas Liu points to how the Internet, which seemed to promise greater freedom for China, has instead become an apparatus of efficient state surveillance and control, Jia and Li show how an exam system with roots that go back to the Sui dynasty roughly 1,400 years ago and that has often been derided for promoting rote learning now works to motivate academic achievement and channel intellectual talent with surprising efficiency. Their book goes on to argue that the gaokao is instrumental in sustaining positive attitudes toward education in China and in at least tempering social and economic inequality.

The Highest Exam compiles a detailed and often dry account of the history and inner workings of what amounts to China’s national college entrance exam, which also serves as the foundation for a more personal discussion of the authors’ backgrounds. Both now teach at elite American universities. Li grew up in Jilin province and scored well on the gaokao in 1989, putting him on a path to eventually becoming codirector of the Center on China’s Economy and Institutions at Stanford.

Jia’s story is more revealing. She was the unwanted daughter of a mother who put her up for adoption, and she had the good fortune to be raised by a middle school teacher in Shandong province. Her rural elementary school had only three teachers, who kept an irregular schedule because they were also working farmers. Despite this, Jia became an avid reader and developed a precocious understanding that newly mastered Chinese characters were worth their proverbial weight in gold. Her father put it to her, “What would you like your future to look like? Would you like to attend vocational school? High school? The choice is yours.”

What the questions reveal is not only the weight that educational and vocational tracking still has in China but also the extent to which test taking determines individual outcomes. Prompted by her father’s question, Jia began to compile an outstanding exam record and eventually got the fourth-highest score in her high school on the gaokao. This in turn enabled her to attend a well-regarded college in Beijing.

For Jia and Li, the gaokao and the tests that lead up to it are far more than their rough American school test equivalents, like the SAT. They form the background of an all-pervading national culture of performance metrics that give life in China something of the quality of a vast and never-ending meritocratic tournament:

The lowest-level employees in the warehouses of a Chinese grocery store chain, who likely never finished high school, have their packing efficiency ranked and displayed on TV screens. At a major Chinese tech firm, when asked whether the employees were ranked against one another, the manager responded with some puzzlement: “Of course.”

In the United States, where there is a deep but folkloric belief in laissez-faire and what people imagine to be equal opportunity, many would doubtlessly bridle at this sort of thing. Jia and Li stop short of proposing any universal applicability of China’s approach to organizing opportunity, or even its outright superiority. But they are not shy about asserting what they see as its merits.

One, they argue, is that the gaokao and other exams allow China to place a premium on the so-called STEM fields—science, technology, engineering, and mathematics—that have been so crucial to the country’s economic advancement in the post-Mao era. Partly because of this, they argue, the return on investment through education has been very high, albeit hard to measure with exactitude. It is also not without costs: “China’s Einsteins may not even test into elite colleges, in part because they may not score well in the non-STEM fields. After all, the gaokao is a composite score.”

They also see competitive test-taking as a partial brake on the further increase of inequality in China, which is already very high. It is all but impossible to attend one of the top universities—Tsinghua, Peking, or Fudan—without previously attending a top high school. But access to both is determined by test scores, not nepotism. Jia and Li posit this as a meaningful advantage over American university admission patterns:

In China, children from the richest 20 percent of families—in other words, the upper class—are 2.3 times more likely to go to an elite college than those from the poorest 20 percent of families—the lower class. Meanwhile in the United States, students from wealthy families are fully eleven times more likely to attend elite institutions than those from poor families.

The system they describe, despite its brutal methods, produces something that much American education does not: genuine mathematical and logical grounding at an early age. What it sacrifices, Jia and Li concede, are the critical thinking skills that American college students cultivate more effectively, along with “social skills that are extremely valuable and likely to become even more so as many tasks become automated.” America’s education system also offers greater opportunity to a broader cross-section of the society, and it is more forgiving of those who don’t begin establishing a record of academic achievement early in life.

These two books introduce useful cautions against easy thinking about China, where cultural and historical inertia run deep in both politics and education. Technologies like the Internet, which the West has long associated with freer expression, have become means of ever-greater state social guidance and control. On the other hand, even with its rigidities, a system of educational benchmarking with roots in antiquity has thus far been made to serve economic advancement rather handily. What no one can know is how long either of these will have such effects.

entries.title: The Virtuoso of Repetition
entries.summary: In both Philip Glass’s most avant-garde and his most commercially successful works, his music seems to accompany some unheard melody while inducing a state of blissful distraction.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Philip Glass assured his place in music history through a breathtakingly simple act of displacement: he took musical gestures that had served for centuries as secondary—busily windmilling arpeggios, stubborn ostinatos, the kind of figures that are more often played by a pianist’s left hand than their right—and treated them as his primary material. Because listeners have been conditioned to think of these as accompaniments, much of Glass’s music has a quality of incompleteness and longing: we cannot help but feel the phantom limb of the absent melody that these figures surely ought to be accompanying.

For this reason, his music thrives in interdisciplinary works, when there actually is some other element in need of musical illumination: a stage picture, a dance, a cinematic scene, a spoken text. By many accounts, Glass is a friendly, obliging collaborator, and his music—fruitfully self-effacing, rarely complex enough to saturate or overwhelm the listener’s attention—behaves the same way. It might be this personality trait that has enabled him to achieve his paradoxical status as an icon of the avant-garde and also one of the most commercially successful of American composers. As he wrote in his memoir, Words Without Music (2015), whenever he is asked how he would define himself, his answer is simple: “I’m a theater composer.”

This statement has the surface banality and hidden abundance of Glass’s best compositions. What does it mean to be a theater composer? It means that one’s music is, from the moment of conception, in dialogue with other media. Music written for the theater cannot demand listeners’ utmost attention; it must tacitly encourage the mind to wander among multiple stimuli.

The foundational paradox of Glass’s career is that the same mysterious qualities—the way his music often seems to accompany some unheard melody, as well as its tendency to precipitate a state of blissful distraction—allowed him to write both his most avant-garde and his most commercial works. His first opera, the nonnarrative Einstein on the Beach (1976), is revolutionary in part because the music, with its fathomless openness, gleefully repels every attempt to parse its meaning. In a Wagner or a Puccini opera, listeners rarely have any doubt about what they’re supposed to be feeling. But the music of Einstein, conceived in tandem with the otherworldly stage pictures of the director Robert Wilson, alternately eases and shocks the listener into a dazed, altered state that is somehow both absorption and distraction. Its task is to denature listeners’ consciousness so that they are maximally receptive to the image before them.

This was a radical approach to opera making. And yet music that maximizes its audience’s receptiveness to an image is also exactly what is required of the soundtrack for a car commercial. Picture it: a shining black luxury SUV driving effortlessly through nighttime rain, a ten-year-old safely cocooned in the leather of the backseat, looking out the window. What else could accompany such an ad but sleek, minor-key Glassian arpeggios?

Since the beginning of his career, Glass has regularly been subjected to an age-old complaint: anyone could write music that’s mostly made of cartwheeling arpeggios outlining only the most rudimentary chord progressions. But as John Cage once said when faced with the accusation that “anyone could do that”: sure they could, but they don’t. Plenty of composers could, in theory, have noticed that a pianist’s left-hand figures can be so pleasurable and comforting to listen to that it might be worth promoting them to center stage, but Glass is the one who actually did.

Any artist who invents a distinctive, instantly recognizable mood is sure to leave a mark on the history of their art form. And Glass did invent a mood, one that feels inseparable from American urban life in the late twentieth century. His unadorned cyclical patterns sometimes exude a chilly, untouchable melancholy; they are sad in the way that ruthlessly optimized, factory-produced luxury goods are sad. Practically none of the composers associated with what has come to be known as minimalism seem to feel especially affectionate toward the label—Glass prefers to call his work “music with repetitive structures”—but the term is a better fit for him than for many others, since he tends to build his music from simple, discrete building blocks: a triad, an ascending minor scale, a slurred two-note pattern. These gestures are endlessly replicable, like Warhol’s soup cans. And the sheen they give off, as they churn along, bespeaks an innocently optimistic vision of modern life as cheerful and outdated as Chicago’s skyline. The harmonies he wields had been available to musicians for many centuries, but the extreme cleanness of his textures—there is no dirt or sweat in his music, no humanizing messiness—could only have been dreamed up in his own time, in a world of cities organized into sleek and separate skyscrapers, cities made mainly of glass.

Apophrades is Harold Bloom’s term, from The Anxiety of Influence (1973), for the uncanny reversal that occurs when an artist has so singular a voice that artists from prior generations seem, in a recurrent temporal flickering, to be imitating them, as when Wallace Stevens seems to be stealing from John Ashbery. Glass has, I think, achieved a kind of apophrades, not with any particular precursor but with the arpeggio itself. These days, if you play a simple, repeated arpeggiated figure, many music lovers are likely to think not of Schubert or Bellini or Beethoven’s “Moonlight” Sonata but of Philip Glass.

The arc of Glass’s six-decade musical career has been on my mind because of the world premiere, on July 5, of his newest orchestral work, his Symphony No. 15, Lincoln, which was performed at Tanglewood by the Boston Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Karen Kamensek, and the baritone Zachary James. This work’s path to the concert stage proved unexpectedly difficult. It was originally commissioned by the National Symphony Orchestra and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in honor of the center’s fiftieth anniversary, in 2022. Had the work been completed on schedule, it would have premiered midway through the Biden administration, at a moment that looks in hindsight like the eye of the storm. But it was not, and its unveiling was postponed to the spring of 2026, by which time the Trump administration had seized control of the Kennedy Center and attempted, grotesquely, to rename it after Trump himself.

Glass would have been justified in pulling his new piece from the Trump-stained Kennedy Center even if it were an abstract instrumental composition. There was all the more reason to do so, however, with a vocal symphony that sets several of Abraham Lincoln’s canonical speeches and that feels like a latter-day echo of Aaron Copland’s Lincoln Portrait (1942), which the BSO performed at Tanglewood alongside this new symphony. One could imagine finding a way to treat the performance of such a piece in the midst of Trump’s Washington as a form of protest. But the composer understandably felt that “the values of Kennedy Center today are in direct conflict with the message of the symphony,” as he wrote in a letter to the National Symphony, and the premiere was deferred once again.

In the end, Glass’s new symphony premiered fifty years to the month after the first performance of Einstein on the Beach, in Avignon, France, in July 1976. I’ve never experienced Einstein in the theater, but whenever I return to the achieved innocence of its music, I find myself refreshed and replenished with creative energy. To listen to certain sections of Einstein—“Train 1,” for instance—is to encounter what sounds like an extraterrestrial preschool’s worth of alien toddlers let out for recess, running around and shrieking with the sheer joy of being alive on whatever their home planet is.

Three quarters of the way through the twentieth century, decades after Albert Einstein’s theories had inadvertently enabled the creation of unimaginably toxic, potentially world-destroying weapons, American society was, it’s safe to say, pretty thoroughly disillusioned with any notion that scientific and technological progress leads mainly to wholesome outcomes. And at a far more modest level, new-music aficionados had been confronted for decades with ever more complex musical systems, harmonic frameworks that sometimes aspired to an Einsteinian upending of the musical cosmos. (What is serial music if not an insistence on totalizing relativity?)

For both ailments, Einstein on the Beach was a tonic. Its simplest gestures—the counting out of numbers until the meaning drains from their names; the giddy, light-speed repetition of familiar harmonic patterns—mark a return to fundamentals. In this work, Glass and Wilson pick up the basic ingredients of music and mathematics—time and space—and wash them in some bright stream.

Einstein is blessed, in practically every bar, with the curiosity and neuroplasticity of a year-old baby; or maybe we, the listeners, are the baby and the piece is a parent who lovingly, attentively shows us the world. These are your hands. These are your feet. These are numbers: one-two-three-four-one-two-three one-two-three-four-one-two-three. This is an octave, a third, a fifth; this is an arpeggio. (Einstein’s sonic texture, shot through with the cheerful candor of those brightly blazing Seventies synthesizers, is somehow inseparable, in my mind, from early episodes of Sesame Street.) Theodor Adorno once wrote, with grudging admiration, that Stravinsky’s orchestrations were so uncannily natural that “the voices of his instruments are like animals whose very existence seems to express their names.” In Einstein, it is not the instruments but music’s essential materials that seem to say their names, announcing themselves as if for the first time. This is one of those precious works of art where it will always be morning.
