A few years ago, in these pages, I discussed the rare cases in which composers find an operatic subject that suits them so perfectly that the characters and events of the drama seem to be emanations from the inner workings of their music.1 Any composer can hope for this kind of immaculate alignment once in a career, if they’re lucky. Glass had the good fortune of achieving this unity of music and subject matter with his second opera, Satyagraha (1980), a luminous depiction of crucial moments in the life of Mahatma Gandhi.2

The composer knew from an early date that Gandhi’s life and teachings would be fruitful terrain for his music: he proposed Gandhi as a subject in his first discussions with Wilson for the piece that ultimately became Einstein. Wilson wasn’t interested, and so Satyagraha is the first Glass opera in which the composer’s mature style is unshadowed by Wilson’s magnetic and quietly dominant sensibility.

Satyagraha (the Sanskrit term could be translated as “truth force” or “the insistence on truth”) is composed of a series of tableaux from Gandhi’s life, including his time at the South African ashram known as Tolstoy Farm and the moment when thousands of his followers (Satyagrahis) took a collective vow to resist a prejudicial government decree. The opera’s three acts correspond to past, present, and future, and each features a figure who influenced Gandhi’s philosophy or was influenced by it: Leo Tolstoy presides over the first act, Gandhi’s contemporary Rabindranath Tagore appears in the second, and the third is infused with the presence of Martin Luther King Jr., an emissary from a future when storm clouds still hang heavy and so much work remains to be done.

Those who have criticized the opera for failing to reckon with the complexities of Gandhi’s biography—“Satyagraha does not bring us much closer to Gandhi’s complicated personality or to his far-from-simple political ideals,” Donal Henahan complained in a New York Times review of the American premiere—miss the point. Satyagraha is not a biopic. The music is itself an act of nonviolent resistance; it enacts the inner process of self-fortification that would be required to participate in a Gandhian political action. Yes, it changes only subtly for many minutes on end, but if you’re going to undertake, say, a twenty-four-day protest march, you have to be willing to perform the same action for a very long time, even if that action is simply walking or calmly taking up space. No sit-in, boycott, or strike would be effective if it only lasted a few minutes, nor would it be effective to abruptly change tactics midway through the action.

This is what makes Satyagraha the ideal Glass opera: here and here only did he find a subject that demands music that peacefully, implacably persists and does little else. Most Western listeners are unlikely to understand the opera’s Sanskrit libretto, but who could fail to understand the meaning of that gentle minor scale that the flutes play in “Tolstoy Farm,” that simple gesture of ascent that must raise itself up, over and over?

Though Satyagraha is a sublime piece, certain technical problems emerge in it that hadn’t been present in the early works that Glass composed for the Philip Glass Ensemble. Satyagraha was the first score that the composer, in his early forties at the time, had written for a conventional orchestra or operatic ensemble since his student days two decades earlier, and this lack of experience sometimes shows. Glass tends to write for every instrument, including the voice, as if it were a synthesizer; there are passages for wind instruments and singers that remain in a brutally high range for a brutally long time.

It’s puzzling that Glass writes such unidiomatic, audibly punishing sections in his operas, because if his music is to achieve its hypnotic effect, it has to sound effortless. Its textures must be unbroken; one cycle of a phrase must flow with mandalic seamlessness into the next. And even in a good performance, there are passages in Satyagraha and its successor, Akhnaten (1984), that are likely to sound sweaty and borderline desperate. Some vocal sections are voiced so densely, in such a high range, that the texture grows clotted with thick agglomerations of choral sound. The resulting grandiosity is surely unintentional. This kind of effect, unfortunately, became all the more frequent in the orchestral music he wrote in subsequent decades.

Whatever happened to the curious, playful infant consciousness of Einstein on the Beach? Sad to say, that infant grew up and got a corporate job. The arpeggios that in Glass’s early works shine like gold in a stream later circulate like mere money. His music’s evolution over the past four decades, which feels less like growth than entrenchment or congealment, is on full display in his symphonies.

Though Glass only began composing symphonies in his mid-fifties, he has now written fifteen, a figure that sounds high until you consider that he has also written more than thirty operas. “Symphony” is a slippery term—it’s been a couple of centuries since the word briefly had a somewhat stable definition as a three- or four-movement work for orchestra with no soloists—and Glass has achieved his symphonic tally in part by gathering an unusually motley collection of pieces under that label: Symphony No. 12, Lodger, is essentially an album of orchestrated songs, while Symphony No. 14, Liechtenstein Suite, is a modest eighteen-minute suite for string orchestra.

As a self-professed theater composer most comfortable writing music that wafts up from an orchestra pit or floats above cinematic images, Glass has expressed some anxiety about placing his music in the concert stage’s unforgiving spotlight: he acknowledged in his memoir that he’s surely “one of the all-time late starters among symphony composers” and that “after years of writing for theater and opera, it was a real jolt for me to drop all of the extramusical content.” Glass has written some successful nonprogrammatic concert music; in the hands of a sensitive pianist, his many solo-piano études can cast a sustained, crystalline spell. But few of his symphonies are among his stronger pieces. In his operas and film scores, I appreciate the music’s welcoming, informal quality, the way it invites the listener’s mind to come and go as it pleases. But symphonies asks listeners for undivided focus of a kind that Glass’s music can’t always sustain.

To write about these symphonies is to run up against a limit of critical language. Many of Glass’s symphonies are at the same time hilariously bad and also sort of delightful. The challenge is that it’s all too easy to point out the features that make them ridiculous, whereas the things that make them enjoyable lie at a sublinguistic level. Even when they’re irritatingly brainless, they are exceptionally pleasant to listen to. They sometimes sound like massage parlor music—in several of them, the harp cloyingly doubles the strings’ melodies—but they also have the effect of a good massage. If I am driving, or folding laundry, or out for a run, a Glass symphony makes the time pass fleetly and fluidly. Only rarely is an idea so crashingly awful that it breaks the reverie. This is music that rewards sustained distraction.

If you depart the realm of pure ASMR and turn on your brain, however, you’ll notice that Glass’s most familiar and beloved gestures can sound slightly grotesque when they’re transplanted to an orchestra. His symphonies sometimes sound like a double parody: they seem to be self-mockery, a bombastic satire of his pioneering early works, and they’re also a send-up of the entire canon of orchestral music. Those fastidiously clean arpeggios and repeated rhythmic figures, so thrillingly sleek when they’re played by synthesizers and saxophones, sound clumsy and self-important when they’re rendered by gigantic string and brass sections. At the same time, to ask an orchestra to play such gestures ad nauseam is, somehow, to ridicule the very apparatus of the orchestra. The cymbals go crash! crash! crash! The triangle goes ding! ding! ding! The whole thing seems to be saying symphony! symphony! symphony!

More than one listener has noticed a kinship between Glass’s symphonies and those of Anton Bruckner, a connection that has been further underlined by the composer’s long collaboration with the Bruckner Orchestra Linz and its former chief conductor Dennis Russell Davies. I think Bruckner is indeed Glass’s most important symphonic forebear, and the best evidence for this is the way that these two composers demand practically identical qualities of the musicians who perform their works. Above all, musicians who play Bruckner and Glass need to be extraordinarily patient. It is deceptively easy for an orchestra to doom a performance of either composer’s work by ratcheting up the tension too quickly or adopting an excessively passionate affect. Bruckner’s symphonies, like Glass’s, can easily sound like empty parodies of symphonic bombast if they’re badly played.

The second most important quality for performing Glass and Bruckner symphonies is beauty of sound. Some composers’ works can sound exciting even when they’re played by a mediocre ensemble: Beethoven’s symphonies teem with so many memorable melodies, so many astonishing twists and turns, that they’re hard to ruin. But Bruckner and Glass symphonies are effective only if they’re played by the very best orchestras, ensembles with a gleaming, burnished sound. The musical material may not seem especially interesting moment by moment, but when played by a great orchestra, the cumulative effect can be magnificent.

These composers’ symphonies also share an unusual harmonic austerity, a quality that can frustrate music lovers who turn to symphonies for a certain kind of tension and release. “Look, there are no real orgasms in Bruckner’s music,” Leonard Bernstein once declared in exasperation. (He was surely contrasting Bruckner with his climax-happy favorite, Mahler.) Bernstein is right that the musical dramas enacted in Bruckner’s symphonies are awesome in scale but enigmatically sexless; when the music gets agitated, it gets louder and louder, jumps up and down, and then, more often than not, stops in its tracks and falls silent. It does not ripplingly crash ashore, as happens so often in Mahler’s symphonies.

In Glass’s symphonies, not only are there no orgasms, I can’t discern any sexual energy. There does not seem to be a self, an ego, present at all; the musical voice emanates from some other region of consciousness. Glass’s harmonies, like Bruckner’s, are often clerically austere; his chords seem to have just returned from a silent meditation retreat that has scrubbed them of all yearning. They are mostly free of dissonant, layered harmonies whose tension might evoke desire or subjectivity or uncertainty.

It never fails to surprise me that early in his career Glass collaborated closely with Samuel Beckett and that his music’s repetitive structures were inspired in part by the effect of Beckett’s plays. As he noted in his memoir, Beckett’s Play “provided no clue as to what the emotional shape of the music might be…. What I noticed during the run was that, from one night to the next, my experience of the theatrical event was substantially different, depending on how my attention was functioning. The epiphany—the emotional high point—came in different places,” and the music therefore had to be “an accomplice in triggering a moving epiphany.” This openness of form, the absence of an obvious climax or catastrophe, is what makes Glass’s early works—especially his works of music theater—so refreshing. The trouble with the symphonies is that he has maintained this formal indeterminacy (there are no obvious climaxes) but conjoined it with an instrumental and gestural palette of all too conventional grandeur.

These symphonies are most effective when their mood is serene, benevolent, or tranquil, and when their scale is modest; it’s no coincidence that the strongest among them, the sly and strange Symphony No. 3, is scored for strings alone. When Glass reaches for clangorous symphonic effects, there is an unbridged gap between the cool, unambiguously major- or minor-key harmonies, with their disinclination to development or transformation, and the sheer bombast of the sound. In the louder moments, the listener is left asking a question that the best music renders irrelevant, impossible to even formulate: Why is this happening?

Abraham Lincoln has appeared recurrently throughout Glass’s body of work across more than forty years: he is a character in the

CIVIL war

S, a multiform Robert Wilson collaboration from the early 1980s; The Perfect American (2013), an opera whose title refers to Walt Disney but that features a role for an animatronic Lincoln; and the opera Appomattox (2007, revised 2015). Glass has always been attracted to political and intellectual leaders possessed of an unbreakable, wayward stoicism—Gandhi, Akhenaten, Kepler—and Lincoln is an ideal American representative of this lineage. I wish I could report that the Lincoln Symphony represents a Falstaff-like resurgence of creative energy or the arrival of the inscrutable, newly childlike innocence that marks Dmitri Shostakovich’s fifteenth and final symphony. Alas, Glass’s fifteenth is one of his weaker efforts.

Glass and his collaborator Stokes Howell have gathered a beautifully varied selection of Lincoln’s oratory: the text includes self-effacing autobiographical anecdotes as well as soul-shaking pronouncements on the irreducible wrong of slavery. You wouldn’t know this from the music, however, which seems mostly oblivious to the text it sets. There is an extreme paucity and poverty of musical ideas; the music simply trundles forward, blurrily impervious to every Lincolnian shift in tone. Lincoln’s account of his brief, unheroic military career—his toughest battles, he tells us, were with the mosquitoes—is endearing and funny, but there’s not an ounce of wit in the accompanying music, which toots solemnly along, its dully burnished mid-tempo arpeggios indistinguishable from the music of an earlier section in which Lincoln darkly warns against the possible rise of an American tyrant.

Later the music’s indifference to the text becomes borderline offensive: after an a cappella spoken rendition of Lincoln’s condemnation of slavery (“If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong”), the ensemble eases into an incomprehensibly mild, toothless moderato, orchestral elevator music. The spoken sections are, however, more effective than the sung ones, since Glass’s text setting is unrelentingly awkward. “In my tenth year I was kicked [pause] by a horse [pause] and was killed [pause] for a time,” Lincoln sings at one point, stopping every three syllables as if out of breath. Lincoln was a young man when he wrote many of these speeches—he delivered the Lyceum Address when he was twenty-eight—and yet Glass, in his setting of them, has managed to make one of America’s greatest orators sound tired, tiresome, and slightly confused.

Glass’s percussion writing has always been a liability in his orchestral music: the percussion gestures are so unimaginative and their timbres so unintegrated with the rest of the ensemble that they often sound like electronically generated MIDI instruments. In this piece, the percussion parts seem to have been chosen by some random instrument generator. Why, in one movement, is a shaker shimmying alongside Mr. Lincoln? When he recounts stories from his youth, why does a triangle ding insistently behind him? Why is his somber farewell address accompanied by the cheerful, chirping two-step of tambourine and wood blocks?

Midway through the premiere, feeling distressed, I thought to myself: but surely this piece has a strong connection to Satyagraha, a piece I love, and its depiction of Gandhi leading his followers through analogous moments of political and spiritual crisis. Why does Satyagraha work so beautifully while this one falls flat? Had I somehow misremembered Satyagraha? Or—oh no—does my admiration for Satyagraha depend on the fact that I don’t speak Sanskrit? If I did, might I be as put off by Glass’s text setting in that piece as I’m bothered by his treatment of English? One of Glass’s most brilliant moves, back in the days of Einstein, was to substitute the simple counting out of numbers for a conventional operatic libretto. Might there be an inverse relationship between a Glass text’s comprehensibility and its aesthetic power?

I returned to Satyagraha and felt relieved: it really is a masterpiece. It is patient, luminous, and wise. Each scene possesses an inner musical current, simple and strong, and Glass lets each idea unfold across broad, rippling plains of time. His new symphony, by contrast, interrupts itself every few minutes, seemingly out of uncertainty or embarrassment. To paraphrase his collaborator Samuel Beckett, this is music that churns on, having no alternative, saying nothing new.

In an interview in 1999 on NPR’s Fresh Air with Ira Glass, who happens to be his cousin, Glass once reflected that “the real issue, I’ve always said to younger composers, it’s not how do you find your voice but how to get rid of it. Getting the voice isn’t hard, it’s getting rid of the damn thing.” In reality, though, a composer can’t aspire to “get” a musical voice like Glass’s. His instantly recognizable voice is a blessing (though he acknowledges that at times it tilts into being a curse) that is inextricable from his singular personality, composed as it is of fruitfully contradictory elements: his likable, disarmingly plainspoken sensibility, his Buddhism-infused worldview, his canny business sense, and his understanding of what was missing in the classical music market. It’s a distinctly American bundle of contradictions, and by now it’s hard to imagine American music without Glass’s voice as a stubbornly vital ingredient. His great early works, Einstein above all, had the impact of an asteroid crashing into earth. And if, in subsequent decades, he’s had trouble digging himself out of a crater, it’s a crater that, through the sheer force of that early vision, he created himself.

entries.content:
Satan’s Harvest Home, an anonymous pamphlet published in London in 1749, offers a copious accounting of contemporary vices, with special attention to “the Present State of Whorecraft, Adultery, Fornication, Procuring, Pimping, Sodomy, And the Game at Flatts.” That state was strong, the pamphlet found, throughout “this good Protestant kingdom” and especially in the capital city of London: brothels bustling, coffeehouses, taverns, and gin shops overflowing, homosexuality on the rise, and the streets filled with a “vast Body of Courtezans, which stands ready, on small Purchase, to obey the Laws of Nature, and gratify the Lust of every drunken Rake-hell.” The unhappy results were, likewise, everywhere to be discerned: livelihoods, marriages, and reputations lost; illegitimate children gotten. Worst of all was “the Propagation of that infectious Disease call’d the French Pox, which in two Centuries has made such incredible Havock all over Europe.” Soldiers, university students, and dissolute aristocrats were notoriously prone to it—as, of course, was the vast body of courtesans—but no one was immune: “Men give it to their Wives; Women to their Husbands, or perhaps their Children; they to their Nurses, and the Nurses again to other Children; so that no Age, Sex or Condition, can be entirely free from the Infection.”

The pamphlet’s rhetoric was sensational but as the historian Olivia Weisser’s new book suggests, its epidemiology was sound. The disease we call syphilis did, in fact, become endemic in Europe at the end of the fifteenth century and menaced the continent for centuries after. Where syphilis came from—whether it was carried north by mercenaries in the army of Charles VIII, was brought from the New World on ships, or evolved domestically from an existing strain of disease—is still unclear. Whatever its origin, the disease’s impact was enormous: the first documented outbreak occurred in Naples in 1495; by the start of the sixteenth century “the dreaded pox”—to quote Weisser’s title—had spread across the continent of Europe and was making inroads in Asia. With its rapidly swelling, close-quartered, highly transient population, the city of London was an ideal breeding ground for venereal disease; by the late eighteenth century roughly one in five city dwellers under the age of thirty-five had been infected, “well over twice as high” as in less crowded regions of the country.

The author of Satan’s Harvest Home was right on another point, too, Weisser suggests: the pox plagued everyone in eighteenth-century London. For those infected with the disease, it meant years of terror and an intermittent, ever-worsening array of symptoms, from skin lesions and genital secretions to bone loss, organ damage, and madness. For the rest of the population, it meant existing in a constant state of low-level anxiety about the possibility of infection. “The disease walked the streets in the form of pocked faces, wigs, patches, and bleached skin,” Weisser writes.

Advertisements for cures adorned the walls of shops and peppered the pages of newspapers. The disease was the subject of drinking songs and the centerpiece of court cases. Antivenereal pills and potions were concocted in home kitchens and stocked in cabinets, while ready-made cures were sold out of grocers’ stalls, markets, bakeries, and cheese shops. City dwellers saw, read, sang, and spoke about venereal disease. To traverse London was to glimpse a kind of long-running public morality play in which the wages of sexual sin were made manifest in the flesh of passersby. But it was also to witness the birth of a new era of medical diagnosis and legal evidence in which the old social currencies of guilt and shame were put to novel uses.

The cloud of infamy surrounding the pox informed the way the disease was treated, both by those afflicted with suspicious symptoms and by those promising to cure them. Indeed, earlier than most histories of medicine suppose, Weisser argues, the pox shifted the understanding of disease itself from the dysregulation of an individual body—a complex ecology of nerves and humors subject to environmental influences and its own peculiar internal weather systems—to the operation of a distinct and recognizable agent of infection. That theoretical shift, which was accompanied in practice by a turn from self-reported symptoms to clinical observation and targeted diagnosis, is typically traced to the urban hospital wards of the nineteenth century, where physicians treating large numbers of patients suffering similar courses of disease started to extrapolate from common symptoms to shared underlying afflictions, and from shared afflictions to standardized regimes of treatment.

The doctors, apothecaries, and unlicensed healers who treated sexually transmitted diseases in eighteenth-century London were not, Weisser emphasizes, thinking in such abstract terms; rather they were confronting an impasse in communication. “Venereal healers relied on sensory observations and manual manipulations to evaluate the sick people in front of them…not because they could envision the disease’s trajectory and knew how to interpret signs with certainty” but because they assumed their patients were lying to them—about what they were feeling, how long they had been suffering, and what actions or events had preceded the onset of their affliction. By the same token, patients themselves sought out ready-made drugs and standardized courses of treatment not because they understood them to be pharmacological specifics for a given pathogen but because they craved anonymity. Old-fashioned morality begot newfangled medical practices.

Advertisement

As a result, Weisser argues, sexually transmitted infections were the first ailments recognized as belonging to their own distinct category of disease, though eighteenth-century diagnostics were far less precise than our own. What we would now regard as different pathogens—chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis—were all simply known as “venereal disease” or, more euphemistically, “the secret disease,” “the French disease,” “the Neapolitan disease,” and “the pox.” (People in France and Naples “preferred other names.”) The disease was understood to manifest on a spectrum of affliction: “a clap” was a mild or early case—the sort of thing a rakish young man might boast about to his friends—while a “true pox” was a serious case, attributed either to repeated acts of sexual excess or to prolonged neglect. (As Alexander Pope said of an acquaintance whose offensive manners had worsened with age, “Time…at last matures a clap to pox.”)

Symptoms varied: in the early stages of a clap, painful urination and genital discharges (“gleets”) were common, as were swellings or eruptions on the skin—“pustules, ulcers, itching, and scabs.” Patients afflicted with the pox might also complain of sore throats and sore eyes, headaches and fevers, symptoms hard to distinguish from those of other ailments (and increasing the temptation, no doubt, to pretend that one merely had a hangover or a cold). In the most advanced cases, however, the signs were unmistakable—and appalling. Sufferers presented with fallen palates, sunken noses, necrotizing sores, mental disturbances, and full bodily paralysis: “a dismal Scene,” in the words of one expert.

The pervasiveness of such dismal scenes in eighteenth-century medical literature and popular culture has led some historians to identify it as a time of unprecedented sexual license. But caution is advisable: “It is impossible to say what individual patients ‘actually’ suffered from,” the historian Kevin Siena observes in Venereal Disease, Hospitals and the Urban Poor (2004), and unwise in any case to link the spread of venereal disease to changes in sexual norms and behaviors.1 What demonstrably did change between the late fifteenth century and the eighteenth was syphilis itself. Records of early outbreaks suggest a nightmarishly swift and vicious disease, as Jared Diamond notes in Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997): “Its pustules often covered the body from the head to the knees, caused flesh to fall off people’s faces, and led to death within a few months.” Within fifty years, however, the spiral-shaped syphilis bacterium had evolved into the agent of a still-nightmarish but far less deadly infection, long incubating and intermittently surfacing. For the bacterium itself, Diamond notes, this was all to the good: “Syphilis spirochetes that evolved so as to keep their victims alive for longer were thereby able to transmit their spirochete offspring into more victims.” For people, however, it meant that dying from the pox was now only half the problem; first, one had to figure out how to live with it.

And that, Weisser argues, is what eighteenth-century Londoners became extraordinarily practiced at doing. Keeping an infection secret wasn’t easy. Beauty patches and thickly applied cosmetics could mask facial lesions and scars, but the wide-stance gait of an individual with an active case of genital sores was harder to dissemble. One man caught running down the street with a stolen silver tankard stuffed down his pants was described in court as “straddling as if he had got the Pox.” In advanced cases—often exacerbated by treatment with toxic mercury-based remedies—ulcers on the throat and palate caused a distinctive speech impediment one healer described as “snuffling.” Snuffling and straddling, the victims of venereal disease were desperate for relief—and for secrecy, which made them easy marks for the purveyors of ready-made cures.

The pox, as the medical historian William F. Bynum puts it, was a “quack’s paradise.” A less censorious name for such practitioners—the one they themselves embraced—is “empirics.” Unlike surgeons and apothecaries, empirics had no formal medical training, no system of apprenticeship or credentialing. Their cures—powders, oils and potions, balms and salves, poultices, pumices, and fumigations—were based not on academic theory but on experience: their own, and the ones they provided to customers, which tended to be dramatically purgative. “As patients retched, defecated, and spat,” Weisser writes, “the pestilence was expelled from their bodies [in] a healthful and observable elimination of excessive, clogged, or corrupt matter.” Feeling awful was proof that the treatment was working. So was paying through the nose: a basic powder could be had for a half-shilling a dose, but a glass-bottled elixir might cost twenty-one shillings—“eleven days’ wages for a skilled tradesperson.” One enterprising healer offered remedies on a sliding scale: “five shillings for a mild clap and up to ten for a severe case.”

Advertisement

Coffeehouse walls were pasted thickly with advertisements for exotic-sounding cures—“Paris pills,” “Greek Water,” “the Herculean Antidote,” the “Italian bolus”—highlighting their provenance and efficacy (“Ancient & Excellent”) and their palatability (“more like a Pomander than a Pill”). The cures themselves could be found for sale at apothecaries and surgeries but also in bookstalls, toy shops, taverns, and private homes. Some pox remedies, conveniently, doubled as treatments for inoffensive ailments: those in need of a discreet cure were urged to go to Mr. Haines on the Strand and “ask for the Three chemical Indian Beads for the Rheumatism.”

Privacy was essential to patients, but for those treating venereal disease, publicity was king. John Case (“your old Friend Dr. Case, who faithfully Cures the Grand P—”) was one big name in the business; John Marten, author of a number of best-selling books on the subject, was another. Dr. William Cockburn—the ad copy writes itself—specialized in “looseness” but had a lucrative sideline in an antivenereal drink “popular among Dutch physicians.” All insisted that they were reputable and trustworthy professionals while their colleagues were rapacious frauds: a substantial chunk of Marten’s A Treatise of All the Degrees and Symptoms of the Venereal Disease, in Both Sexes (1708) is devoted to the “Mischiefs caus’d by Ignorant Pretenders.”

In another book, Marten impugned one rival, John Spinke, by name, calling him a “Country-barber” and his remedies a “meer Sham to get Mony.” Spinke retaliated with a self-published volume titled Quackery Unmask’d (1711), in which he charged Marten—“Venus’s Botcher” and “Quack of Quacks”—with faking his learning, juking his book sales, and “talking like a tampering Old Woman.” A century earlier, in the records he kept of his busy medical practice in Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare’s son-in-law John Hall complained that a man with “virulent gonorrhea” had wasted a month seeking remedies from a surgeon before coming to him to be “suitably and correctly purged.”2

Anonymized accounts of successful treatments were a crucial marketing device for healers, and these supply Weisser with some of her most detailed evidence of how venereal disease reshaped doctor–patient relations. Practitioners called in to consult on possible cases of the pox took for granted that their patients would obfuscate, prevaricate, and hedge, and so they paid close attention both to their outward symptoms and to their “Habit and State of Life.” In an elderly spinster a recurring sore throat might be a “common Catarrh or Cold,” but in a known denizen of brothels and bathhouses, it was probably a clap. One patient first attributed his swollen testicle to having slept cross-legged, but when the physician Daniel Turner—who had obtained a medical degree from Yale in exchange for a donation of books to the college’s fledgling library—noticed stains on his bedsheets, the man burst into tears, “admitting that he was poxed and begging Turner to protect his reputation.”

In the encounter between Turner and his patient, Weisser sees an anticipation of the moralizing logic of the nineteenth-century penitentiary, Magdalen hospitals, and other “reform-minded institutions,” although, as she acknowledges, pox treatment also had the aura of the pre-Reformation Church. The box constructed to shield customers from public view while they paid for pills handed through a tavern window strongly resembled a confessional, and even when a healer was sure of his diagnosis the patient’s admission of sexual impropriety was regarded as salutary. But savvy practitioners understood that it behooved them not to insist on a full confession, much less perfect contrition, before proceeding to absolution in pill or powder form. “I never differ with patients about names,” the physician John Douglas explained, “but leave them always to call their disease what they please.”

Of course, plenty of sufferers sought to cure themselves—the most private method of all. Weisser notes that early modern recipe books are a valuable but “elusive” resource for tracking trends in the treatment of venereal disease, since few recipes are baldly titled “for the pox.” But home remedies for dropsy, scurvy, and bone ache often contain knowing allusions to what the compiler of one recipe book called “diseases in the secret parts”; references to warts, sores, or “runnings,” “pain and rawness of the privities,” and “swellings in the yard” supplied broad hints to those in need. Ingredients gave hints, too: plantain water, chinaroot, guaiacum seeds, and sarsaparilla were known specifics for venereal disease; so were breast milk and liquid or powdered mercury. One Sussex man “made himself a mercurial girdle”—flannel coated in ointment made of mercury, turpentine, and pig fat—and wore it for a month to treat an itch he attributed to “lying on dirty bedsheets.”

The most inventive and inveterate self-treater of venereal disease Weisser finds is Thomas Thistlewood, a Lincolnshire man who moved to Jamaica in 1750, serving first as an overseer and then as the owner of a sugar plantation. Thistlewood was a horror of a human being, an appallingly cruel and violent man whose sadistic instincts were licensed and supercharged by the system of slavery.3 He was also a diligent diarist who kept careful track of the progress of the venereal disease he had brought with him from England and of his yearslong quest for a cure. The list of Thistlewood’s recurring symptoms is, frankly, a joy to contemplate: “sores and swellings on his groin, a burning sensation while urinating, involuntary erections, small fleshy growths on his genitals, and continued discharges”; muscle aches, headaches, and fevers; a “sort of tickling in the urethra,” bouts of “searing pain,” and a “weeping” penis. The hellish remedies he endured also make for pleasant reading: mercury pills and turpentine enemas, regular bloodletting and gallons of home-brewed herbal emetics, self-administered exams with a metal probe, injections of “cleansing water” into the urethra with an ivory syringe, poultices made of nettles and “cow itch.” It isn’t clear from the diary whether Thistlewood ever attempted a cure involving the application of powdered quicklime dissolved in boiling water, “as hot as y[o]u can endure it,” to genital sores—but one can hope.

What is hard to bear is the knowledge that Thistlewood was spreading his disease to the victims of his relentless sexual predation. In his diary he routinely mentions forcible encounters with enslaved women—at least 138 of them, by his own account. Plantation records reveal that twenty-eight of those women suffered subsequent venereal infections. Predictably, Thistlewood blamed the women. “Head ach[e], feverish feel oddly: a small running,” he writes in one entry, adding, “suspect Fanny.”

Despite its title, the early chapters of The Dreaded Pox are strikingly buoyant in tone, leavened by the Entrepreneurial Anticks of quacks and the follies and foibles of their customers. Eighteenth-century English folk also thought venereal disease was funny: in ballads, jest books, and plays, the tricksy, poxy whore and her hapless (or hard-bitten) john were recurring comic types. Real-life accounts of affliction sold even better: as one critic of John Marten’s medical treatises shrewdly observed, he wrote to “amuse the World and gain Patients.” The first aim was, potentially, every bit as lucrative as the second, and the cheerfully lurid cover of The Dreaded Pox suggests that Weisser’s own publisher is well aware of it.

But Weisser herself remains attuned to the grim realities of her subject. The pox ruined lives, and as the later chapters in her book remind us, not everyone had a rollicking good time on the way to getting it. Popular imagination associated the pox with prostitutes, but as the author of Satan’s Harvest Home lamented, mothers and nursemaids also sometimes transmitted the disease to children. Indeed, many female sufferers of venereal disease were married women infected by their husbands; others, like the enslaved women of the Thistlewood plantation, were victims of rape. And in both cases, the outward manifestations of the pox, however painful and unwelcome, were also a rare form of legal currency: backed by the validation of a professional diagnosis, they were tangible proofs of harms society otherwise tended to ignore.

Take the case of Lady Frances Hanbury Williams, whose husband, Charles, regularly visited the spa town of Bath, seeking relief from what he described as a stubborn case of colic. In fact, it was a venereal disease—as Lady Frances realized in late August 1742, when she found herself in “misserable condition” back in London, suffering from painful genital ulcers and a persistent vaginal discharge. When she recovered sufficiently to do so, Lady Frances filed for a legal separation and custody of the couple’s two young daughters. Absent “undue cruelty,” a husband’s adultery was not grounds for such a separation, and in letters to her lawyers, Lady Frances never openly accused Lord Charles of infidelity. Instead, she charged him with the “infamous Crime” of lying to her about the nature of his own affliction. The court awarded her the separation, and in 1762, when Lord Charles died, an Act of Parliament gave her the right to revert to her maiden name. A decade later she died under the care of a physician from St. Luke’s Hospital for Lunaticks.

Weisser finds records of seventeen trials in which a wife’s unwitting infection with venereal disease was advanced as legal cause for separation from her husband. Men no doubt found themselves in similar predicaments, infected by their adulterous wives, but they might not have needed to out themselves in court, since a wife’s infidelity was sufficient cause for separation if her husband wanted it. For women, however, venereal disease provided “a language for expressing the grave implications” of sexual betrayal—and a language for expressing the devastation of rape. Unlike firsthand testimony, which was regarded as untrustworthy, and unlike bruises, scrapes, and broken bones, which healed in time, the marks of venereal disease were “long-enduring, debilitating, and visible.”

The qualities that made infection so publicly shameful were singularly useful as evidence: awkward gaits, persistent sores, stained linens, and foul secretions “did the work of proving rape.” The method wasn’t infallible, of course, and establishing that sex has occurred isn’t the same as establishing that it was nonconsensual. But the presence of an affliction no one wanted seems to have made it significantly easier for a judge and jury to grant that the sex had also been unwanted: around 11 percent of early modern rape trials ended in a conviction, but the conviction rate for trials involving venereal disease was 34 percent.

Stigma, then, was the most complicated and unpredictable side effect of all. It added greatly to the suffering and anxiety of many eighteenth-century patients, but it gave others a medically authorized, legally consequential vocabulary for naming sexual harms. For those desperate to avoid it, stigma created huge incentives to disguise or falsify the nature of their affliction. For those eager to capitalize on it, it created a booming trade in quick cures and ready-made remedies—the beginnings, Weisser suggests, of the commercial pharmaceutical industry. And for medical professionals of all stripes, it shifted the burden of attention and care from the individual subjective experience of illness to the underlying causes and recognizable patterns of disease, even as it also recast treatment as a confessional rite. When it came to venereal disease, Weisser’s book persuasively suggests, stigma was both an atavistic force and a cultural accelerant. It was part of what made the pox dreaded, and medicine modern.

entries.content:
It’s not vertigo exactly, more a diagonal feeling

as if a giant had picked up the room and were

about to spill everything, you included.

And then there is the tired-as-Sisyphus feeling

from drawing a load of shadows up a painted hill.

A film of spirits clouds our eyes, making it impossible

to watch the movie. Don’t tell me what happens next.

Can a person already in a trance be hypnotized again?

I need to decide something—anything will do.

It looks about to rain, but I’m going for a walk

to exercise what’s left of my free will.

entries.content:
In 1949 Ithell Colquhoun—artist, writer, and occultist—produced a manifesto, titled “The Mantic Stain,” in which she called on her readers to follow French Surrealism’s practice of “pure psychic automatism.” It was, Breton wrote, “the real working of thought. Dictation of thought, without any control exercised by reason, and beyond any preoccupation, aesthetic or moral.” “Mantic” was a characteristically esoteric flourish on Colquhoun’s part; it’s derived from the ancient Greek for “prophet” or “seer,” as in the arts of divination (by card reading—cartomancy; by dream interpretation—oneiromancy), and alludes to Manto, the daughter of Tiresias, the seer who experienced existence as both male and female. It also pays homage to the praying mantis, an erotic symbol beloved of the Surrealists.

Oracular methods such as automatism and tarot cards would lead Colquhoun down many paths in her search for knowledge, while the duality of the androgyne fascinated her in her art and writing. Mantic staining, including automatic processes like blotting and doodling, was a way anyone could access hidden orders of existence and liberate the inner self and its creative energies:

To a beginner the fact that he is faced not with an empty white rectangle…but with a suggestive chiaroscuro or a colour combination with potentialities will give him confidence. This self-confidence is the first step towards revealing the mind’s profound imaginative riches.

Colquhoun first became aware of the Surrealists in Paris, where she was spending time in the early Thirties, and sat for Man Ray, who portrayed her as a corn goddess, with a sheaf of ripe wheat in her hands and her skirt parted. But it was the first major Surrealist exhibition in London, in 1936, that turned her into a disciple and fervent proselytizer for the movement. She was present at the famous opening when Salvador Dalí, wearing a deep-sea diving suit and holding two wolfhounds on a leash, began giving a lecture and had to be rescued from suffocating to death in the process. Later, back in Paris, Colquhoun met Breton, and in 1939, on the eve of World War II, joined a gathering at the château of Chemillieu, where the artists Roberto Matta and Gordon Onslow Ford took the discussions in a more esoteric direction, which appealed strongly to Colquhoun. She was already taking a serious interest in ritual magic, ancient and novel.

The 1949 essay on the mantic stain reappeared in another version two years later as “Children of the Mantic Stain,” an enthusiastic inventory of the many processes Surrealists had devised to set free the imagination. It includes decalcomania—the folding or pressing of paper onto a pour or splash of ink or paint, a process brilliantly explored by Max Ernst in his apocalyptic landscape paintings of the 1940s, for example Europe after the Rain II (1940–1942). She also describes frottage (taking a rubbing—another method pioneered by Ernst), fumage (holding paper to a flame to scry the traces it leaves), and parsemage, her own invention, which involves sprinkling powdered charcoal or pigment onto water and then passing a sheet of paper under the surface to lift off the image.

The psychologist Hermann Rorschach famously asked patients to “read” inkblots and then analyze their responses. Ernst, Dalí, and other Surrealists took the method further and proposed intervening, heightening with brush and pen what they discerned in the random marks, drawing out dramatic scenarios and dreamscapes. This approach, a modern variation on the ancient divinatory techniques of seeing the future in clouds, animal entrails, or tea leaves, was most passionately adapted by Dalí with his “paranoiac-critical method.” He was a virtuoso at applying it to produce complex—and lasting—phantasmagorias such as The Persistence of Memory (1931) and Metamorphosis of Narcissus (1937).

Colquhoun had a penchant for pedagogy, and in l948 she demonstrated several of these avant-garde methods for a very polite early BBC television documentary, telling viewers how to set free their artistic potential in the same manner as she might have shown how to make an omelet. In her own work, she improvised with them to powerful effect, allowing her vivid pigments to spill and ooze in paintings such as Gorgon (1946), Decalcomania counterpart for “Gorgon” (1946), and Woman of Beare (1950). She also took a significant step when she extended these Daliesque methods to her writing—and in this lies her true originality.

In the novels Goose of Hermogenes and I Saw Water, Colquhoun practices a literary form of mantic staining: fugues of images, sudden gaps and non sequiturs, unexplained exits and entrances, and abolition of cause and effect intensify the strangeness of her female protagonists’ journeys toward transfiguration. Surreal landscapes, as if created by decalcomania, are live with fantastic phenomena and bright with hallucinatory mineral colors. In Goose of Hermogenes, the heroine records:

I now discovered fish-like flowers growing directly from the stone without leaves. I could hardly get foot-hold or hand-hold without crushing or gripping these cold petals, which spread their cherry and blue-grey all about the ascent, a salty deposit covering them with a dusty grape-like bloom.

Later, during the final stages of her apotheosis, she finds, “In this water were strange living creatures, like sea-anemones…. They were of various jewel-colours, ruby, sapphire, emerald, some of them spotted with white.”

Advertisement

Throughout her life Colquhoun kept a dream journal and pored over her records to plan her fictions, tracing patterns to uncover the dreams’ meaning. One particular dream journey in which she found herself in a cave in Nicaragua, a country she had never visited, inspired her to hunt for corroboration from its geography. This katabasis, or descent into the underworld, inspired a striking section of I Saw Water.

From the Surrealist perspective, dreams weren’t the debris of consciousness, and dreaming wasn’t waste disposal performed by the brain in readiness for the light of day. As Breton’s hero Baudelaire wrote in a letter of 1856:

Since you enjoy dreams, here’s one that I’m sure won’t disappoint you. It’s 5 in the morning, so it’s still fresh. Note that this is only one sample from the thousands of dreams that constantly besiege me, and I don’t need to tell you that their complete singularity, and the fact that they are entirely unrelated to my daily activities or my passionate adventures always leads me to believe that they are a kind of hieroglyphic language to which I don’t hold the key.1

Colquhoun believed there was a key and she could find it. She researched cultures in which dreams delivered prophetic truth-telling messages from a higher plane. Like splashes and blots, dreams emanated from hidden forces, perhaps of the human mind, perhaps not. She had a metaphysical belief in their potential to put her in touch with supernatural beings, not angels or demons in any religious sense, nor the fairies or phantoms of popular belief, but spirits posited by mystical systems such as astrology and alchemy, otherworldly manifestations raised by enchanters and magi who had developed means of contacting them.

Accordingly, Goose of Hermogenes progresses up the alchemical ladder as, chapter by chapter, the heroine ascends toward wisdom; in I Saw Water, geomantic figures provide each chapter’s leitmotif (though it must be said that the rationale remains elusive to the reader).

Ithell Colquhoun was born in 1906 in India, where her father, a British colonial officer, had himself been born. (Her unusual first name, Ithell—pronounced Eye-thell—isn’t an obscure spelling of Ethel but a forebear’s surname; her last name is pronounced Kuh-hoon.) Like many servants of the Raj, Colquhoun père wished his daughter to grow up a thoroughly British girl, and she was sent to “the mother country” to be brought up by an aunt in Cheltenham. There, in that respectable Cotswolds spa town, she attended Cheltenham Ladies’ College, where the program had been shaped by the legendary reformers Miss Buss and Miss Beale, and was consequently more ambitious than the usual fare for girls at the time. Ithell was joined by her mother, then went on to the local art college. Her curiosity about magic was encouraged by a cousin, Edward Garstin, who was to publish The Secret Fire: An Alchemical Study (1932) and other occult works. He introduced Colquhoun to Kabbalah and the teachings of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. (W.B. Yeats had been active in the order for a time—Yeats, Ireland, Celtic myth, and visionary poetry would become essential elements in Colquhoun’s oeuvre.)

In 1927 Colquhoun enrolled at the Slade, part of the progressive, secular University College London and the leading art school in the country. At this stage Colquhoun was painting subjects from classical mythology and the Bible; her forms were massive, sculptural, strongly delineated—think William Blake reworked by Tamara de Lempicka—resolutely anti-decorative, and fierce in mood. She favored heroic episodes such as Judith beheading Holofernes and took her own distinct path with others: a strange painting of a scene from Exodus shows Moses rigid in goatskin and horns while Aaron, voluminously robed and coiffed, embraces him passionately. The Slade’s renowned professor, the surgeon-painter Henry Tonks, wrote to her, “You go out to gather strawberries and come back with two strange beetles and a spider instead.”

Colquhoun benefited from a small trust fund, enabling her to live as an independent artist-scholar. Free to choose, she was no idle rentier. A copious stream of poems, tracts, stories, accounts of dreams, and aesthetic theories flowed from her pen. Although she never returned to her birthplace, she hankered after the sights, sounds, and festivals of India, and she became an adept of Indian mysticism, alongside alchemy, astrology, Kabbalah, Egyptian myth, Christian hagiography, and Sufism. She also joined—and left—a bewildering number of groups and secret societies. Her appetite for arcana seems to have been unappeasable. Her art and her fiction visit sites of sacred power, conveyed in works such as Dance of the Nine Opals (1942) and La Cathédrale Engloutie (1952).

Advertisement

Colquhoun had affairs with men and women: a fisher lad in Corsica inspired a chapter in Goose of Hermogenes, and she fell passionately in love with a woman in Greece named Andromaque “Kyria” Kazou, whose strong features she drew and painted several times; the affair inspired a heady story, “Lesbian Shore,” as yet unpublished. She read widely, especially poetry, and translated Mallarmé and Breton. Breton’s style, so influential on her cult of automatism, suffuses the imagery of her own writing. Like many others she longed to achieve the dazzling incoherence of his Fata Morgana—that mantic cataract of a poem—and the audacity and delirious impossibility of its first word picture: “Ce matin la fille de la montagne tient sur ses genoux un accordéon de chauves-souris blanches” (This morning the mountain’s daughter holds on her knees an accordion of white bats).

During the war, Colquhoun lived and worked in London—and it was there, in the early 1940s, that she met Toni del Renzio. An improbable figure of Byronic glamor, he was a Romanov on his mother’s side and an Italian aristocrat on his father’s (with a bouquet of titles); he had deserted from the Italian army in Abyssinia, joined the Partisans in Spain, abandoned them, and fetched up in London, where he befriended E.L.T. Mesens, the Belgian-born leader of the British Surrealist group. The war had discouraged its members; del Renzio presented himself as ready and willing to regalvanize them.

Colquhoun and del Renzio married in 1943, and for a few years the marriage was turbulent but exciting. Explicit drawings and watercolors she made in this period explode with frank delight, while the series of erotic talismanic figures Diagrams of Love shows her again seeking to pin down the mess and flux of experience in a symbolic system. The possible primal unity of the sexes, as described by Aristophanes in Plato’s Symposium, was a Surrealist motif that gripped Colquhoun; she explored the potential fusion of male and female not only in her art but also in her writing. Goose of Hermogenes and other stories conflate the Greek myth of the original hermaphroditic state of human beings with the androgyne, a longed-for stage in the journey to the philosopher’s stone, the ultimate goal of the alchemical process.

Despite her keen advocacy of surrealism, in 1940 Colquhoun was either expelled from the British group or walked away because, it is generally agreed, she would not give up her esoteric adventures. Mesens wanted to impose his authority, and when he decreed that members of the group could not join any other society, Colquhoun wasn’t sufficiently docile. But whatever the cause of the break, I feel it damaged Colquhoun. It cut her work off from the larger collective endeavor of Surrealism and its psychological inquiries and deepened the marginalization she suffered for decades. The American anthropologist and folklorist Amy Hale, author of an enraptured biography of Colquhoun called Genius of the Fern Loved Gully (2020), observes that

although most historical mentions of Ithell Colquhoun focus on her relationship with the Surrealist movement in Britain, her commitment to occultism was more consequential and, in fact, her Surrealism was in service to that obsession, which was the principal driver of most of her life’s work.

Hale welcomes Colquhoun’s occultism as pioneering feminism, whereas some of her readers and viewers—myself among them—shrink from her earnest commitment to practical magic.

Colquhoun’s marriage to del Renzio disintegrated, and they divorced in 1947. She suffered a period of grave depression and decided to retreat to Lamorna, a celebrated scenic village in the woods on the precipitous Cornish coast. She bought a shack called Vow Cave. It had no plumbing or electricity. Seeing herself as Celtic by ancestry and affinity, she found inspiration in its rugged austerity and settled there for the rest of her life.

The Surrealists idolized Woman and generally belittled actual women: they saw them as femmes-enfants, brides, love objects, praying mantises, sirens, medusas. (The influence of Freud shows strongly!) But in 1985 Whitney Chadwick’s Women Artists and the Surrealist Movement—a brilliant work of feminist recuperation—opened my eyes and the eyes of many others to the lives and work of artists such as Leonora Carrington, Dorothea Tanning, Kay Sage, and Colquhoun.2 Chadwick reproduced Colquhoun’s magnificent, highly perturbing Scylla (1938), a painting of two fleshy pillars rising out of the sea and bracketing a narrow passage, with coral blossoming in the clear water like pubic hair. She also included Colquhoun’s The Pine Family (1940), a grimly comic work that shows three mutilated bodies like pollarded tree trunks lying alongside one another, one labeled, in Magritte-style script, “l’hermaphrodite circoncis” (the circumcised hermaphrodite).

Since Chadwick’s book, there has been a tectonic shift in the fortunes of women artists such as Frida Kahlo, Lee Miller, Louise Bourgeois, Paula Rego, and more. Among Chadwick’s subjects, Carrington received some recognition in her lifetime but did not live to see the global cult she has now inspired (and the prices at auction to match).

Colquhoun has had to wait longer to be fully disinterred from obscurity. At her death in 1988, she left her home and the contents of her studio to the National Trust and specified that her occult material should go to the Tate. The division seems to have paralyzed the beneficiaries, and for many years nothing was done. The photomontage artist Linder, an early fan, visited Lanhydrock, the National Trust property in Cornwall where part of Colquhoun’s legacy had been consigned, and found, to her utter dismay, hundreds of drawings, paintings, and drafts strewn about higgledy-piggledy, uncatalogued, uncherished.

In 2019, more than thirty years after Colquhoun’s death, the thousands of items in her archive were at last properly assembled; interest has been growing ever since, culminating in “Between Worlds,” a vast survey show, which opened at Tate St. Ives, near her home in Cornwall, last year and then traveled—in a slightly trimmed version—to Tate Britain in London. Curated by Katy Norris, who also edited the catalog, the retrospective displayed works from every stage of Colquhoun’s career, including Scylla, The Pine Family, Diagrams of Love, her later explorations of rocks and plants, and leading up to her Taro (her preferred spelling) pack, made in 1977 with a voluptuous use of mantic staining. The artworks were supported by fascinating manuscripts and other ephemera in which Colquhoun dilates on the Goddess, color symbolism, ley lines, astrological alignments, tarot, and sex magic.

Hale vividly describes her first sighting of the material: “dozens of manuscripts, poems, weird magical experiments on graph paper, conjurations of angels, love spells, petitions to healers, colourful tesseracts, magical journals and so, so many letters.” She followed Genius of the Fern Loved Gully with Sex Magic (2024), a catalog of the Diagrams of Love, and has just brought out A Walking Flame, a collection of Colquhoun’s essays on magic and the occult. Hale’s approach confirms a pervasive change in the cultural sphere about the value of witchcraft, magic, paganism, and what is caught under the rubric of “women’s spirituality.”

Attitudes to the Goddess and the Divine Feminine, as expressed by postwar feminists (my generation), have taken a different metaphysical direction. Where we deconstructed the stance of Robert Graves in his 1948 study The White Goddess (while enjoying its lore and learning) and opposed the arguments of Ted Hughes about “The Goddess of Complete Being” in his 1992 study of Shakespeare (while admiring his poetic knowledge), and saw such worship of Woman as saturated with patriarchal notions of whores and virgins, mothers and helpmeets, many women today are reactivating the cult of the Goddess and finding new strength in the idea of the witch and the seer. For example, the small feminist press Spiral House, an imprint of Silver Press, specializes in this new quest for female wisdom, taking it into psychology and ecology, memory and consciousness studies.

In this current turn, Ithell Colquhoun, dream interpreter, tarot reader, and crystal gazer, has emerged as a torch bearer for a definite strand in contemporary culture, which has identified a pantheon of precursors, mediumistic artists across time and place: in Victorian England, Georgiana Houghton photographed spirits and produced startlingly proto-abstract expressionist paintings inspired by her spirit visitors; during the first half of the twentieth century, Hilma af Klint in Sweden had visions and likewise broke with the figurative conventions of her contemporaries; and in Switzerland, Emma Kunz tuned in to the earth’s energy with a pendulum and made subtle geometric paintings. Such artists were once thought of as outliers but they are now inspiring vigorous interest. In 2024 in Cambridge, England, a show called “The Goddess, the Deity and the Cyborg,” selected from the Women’s Art Collection, explored psychic expressions of female power, and a recent major exhibition in Milan, curated by Massimiliano Gioni and others, showed a heterogeneous group of artists past and present—almost every one of them female, and including af Klint, Houghton, and Kunz—united under the sign of Fata Morgana, the fairy and meteorological portent invoked by Breton, and implied that together they expressed the magical unconscious.3 (Colquhoun’s absence was probably caused by her works being shown elsewhere.)

During Colquhoun’s postwar years, she continued to make art but was also writing prolifically—essays, poetry, and a pair of travel books, The Crying of the Wind: Ireland (1954) and The Living Stones: Cornwall (1957), which have recently been reissued along with her novel Goose of Hermogenes. As a travel writer, Colquhoun shows herself to be a fine, lively collector of anecdote and ancient lore. She scrambles over rocks and stomps through briars and nettles, undaunted in her hunt for another holy well, another menhir or stone circle. In The Living Stones, she observes a Druidic gathering with a sharp eye, deploring the practical footwear visible beneath the elders’ ceremonial robes and the reliance on microphones. The necessity to use technological aids, as opposed to the human voice, strikes her as a grim sign of modern decline, our disconnection from nature and its divine energy.

The Living Stones and The Crying of the Wind found readers then, and they are still entertaining and richly informative. Their success persuaded her friend, the independent publisher Peter Owen, to yield to her pleas, and in 1961 he brought out her novel Goose of Hermogenes. The title provides a typically abstruse clue to the narrative: it sounds like a concoction—attar of roses or balm of Gilead—and indeed “goose of Hermogenes” is a rare term for the philosopher’s stone, which may help produce the elixir of life, while “Hermogenes” means “born of Hermes,” the Greek god of hermetic knowledge, codes, and tricks, who in the Roman pantheon is called Mercury, the prime ingredient in the great work of transformation.

The heroine of Goose of Hermogenes is unnamed. At the start, she has been summoned to the island of a mysterious uncle for reasons that aren’t clear. When she arrives, she encounters peculiar inhabitants including an “Anchorite,” who is helpful but appears to be an agent of her uncle’s; later, as she explores farther, she meets several more islanders, each more puzzling than the last. Her uncle, the controlling genius loci, remains hidden in his study until, at their first meeting, he greets her with a mysterious dumb show:

After a few seconds a shutter, not unlike that of a box-office, opened in the middle of the panelling; and in this aperture, illumined from within by a glow faintly rose-coloured, appeared my Uncle’s hands. They held a few leaves from some rare booklet, embossed and illuminated with half-perceived designs. The pages fluttered for a few moments like a butterfly on some fleshy exotic bloom, then the shutter was drawn again and the door darkened.

What does this mean? It is left an enigma. The uncle is a Prospero-like wizard but more sinister. She suspects he is working on a spell to resist death and

I somehow guessed that my Uncle wanted me in his house because of my jewels, which were beautiful as children’s sweets and very precious, and which he probably fancied to be possessed of alchemystic powers. But he had to obtain them from me by some not-too-openly disreputable means, and this was not easy, since I always wore them.

Colquhoun’s protagonist doesn’t want to join in her uncle’s experiments to turn base metal into gold or defy nature by living forever. Like her author, she desires wisdom, which means freedom from the burden of the self in a mystical, Eastern key. But either this uncle’s sorcery or another unseen enchantment of the island binds the heroine so that, like Ferdinand in The Tempest, she cannot escape.

The novel moves through a series of twelve weird tableaux, each named after a stage in the process as drawn up by the influential alchemist George Ripley, beginning with “Calcination” and ending in “Projection.” This structure feels forced, except in the chapter “Conjunction,” which tells a charming, whimsical love-story-cum-fairy-tale: the heroine comes across a manuscript about a pair of doomed young lovers. Oriole, pale and wan, teaches his soulmate Corolla to fly, and in a mystical apotheosis they follow a phoenix:

The bird, too, must have felt a link with the fiery west, for it sailed on as though drawn without volition to plunge into that flaming core; and with this creature of air for guide, the two sailed effortlessly on, desiring no return.

On her pilgrim’s progress, the protagonist continues to roam the island. Colquhoun’s belief in all of nature being alive and sentient, alongside her considerable botanical knowledge, animates the scenery. The plot, such as it is, involves her heroine in horrific ordeals: in the chapter “Exaltation,” she is seized and stripped, bound and drugged, lashed and raped, and offered up, as in some Rite of Spring, to a statue of a faun or Silen: “I laid my mouth to its stoney lips, and a tongue, icy as an adder’s, seemed to dart from between them to meet mine.”

The next morning, she wakes to find herself undamaged. It was all a dream.

Fantasy here is intrinsically incorporeal, and the Sadean tableau another dumb show. This is not only troubling but unsatisfactory—the author appears to be quitting, abandoning the responsibility for what her unconscious has dictated.

In the final, twelfth chapter, she enters the land of the dead, visits the abandoned family home, and in an eerie Dantesque encounter meets her father, who does not know he is dead. She then enters a paradise of plenty, where “warm fountains the colour of port-wine were jetting through the earth, fertilising it to this abundant growth.” Ever the persevering pilgrim, she keeps going, toward “the mountainy country to the east…. The region was far, but even as I looked its pencilled summits were touched by the first auroral glow.” Is this a prompt from the unconscious toward the Golden Dawn, or a deliberate allusion on Colquhoun’s part? Toward the close, the protagonist opens her veins and fuses with the sea in a mystical act of self-annihilation.

The Surrealist scholar Alyce Mahon, who contributes an essay to Between Worlds, sees these tableaux as symbolic and sacramental. Certainly, Colquhoun’s imagination coincides with Catholic ideas of exaltation in violent suffering.

A thirteenth chapter of Goose of Hermogenes, “Hexentanz,” was left out of the 1961 edition and has now been restored. It features another limbless body, the Stump, and evil children who abuse him for fun. I wasn’t convinced by its appearance at the end of the novel, after the heroine has attained alchemical transformation, but it does reveal that Colquhoun could match any outré male Surrealist in provocative sadism.

Her novel I Saw Water—written around 1967 but not published until 2014, in an edition illuminatingly annotated and edited by Richard Shillitoe and Mark S. Morrisson—was entirely composed from her dreams, Colquhoun said, and then later organized into chapters named after a geomantic figure. For example, “Bound” (chapter 5) evokes the figure of “Carcer,” Latin for “prison,” signifying “setbacks and delays.” The stories that result are bizarre, dramatic, not always intelligible.

Although both novels risk sounding like a friend with a hangover recounting a dream, I enjoyed I Saw Water more than Goose of Hermogenes. Colquhoun is at times shrewd in her observation of her characters and can be sly and funny and earthy in a voice closer to Carrington’s. The novel also describes a very real human situation, probably based on her own experience: the husband of one of her principal characters is a charmer, an extravagant wastrel, who is living off his wife’s money and flaunts his love affair with another man. All of this is startlingly frank—at a time when homosexuality was still a crime.

The heroine, Brigid, has entered a convent of the Order of the Ianua Vitae in Ménec, Brittany, where, reluctant to take final vows, she herds the sisters’ cows and strikes up an ambiguous friendship with the novice mistress, Sister Mary Paracelsus, who brews potions in her laboratory from local plants and herbs (and is named for the fifteenth-century Swiss alchemist). Out in the fields, Brigid meets a roguish local landowner and plans to elope with him but is foiled when he drowns—a turn of events she accepts without shedding a tear. A parallel story meanwhile unfolds about Brigid’s cousin Charlotte who, after the collapse of her marriage, is in pursuit of her married psychiatrist. He has a little boy who is suffering from a severe, unnamed disorder. In a healing ritual, inspired by Catholic festivals in Brittany, water from a holy well is sprinkled on the child:

[He] uttered a cry different in tone from any we had yet heard from him and struggled out of his father’s arms. His feet touched the tessellated floor, actually supporting his weight; then he spun round to face the nave, his arms outstretched as if to embrace the crowd. For an instant his strangeness dropped away from him, his face was lit up by a look of lively intelligence and he stood before us as the child he might have been. He took one step forward, then collapsed and lay unmoving, his eyes fixed on the dome alone.

The hope of a miracle cure, and the subsequent sadness and disillusionment, are very affecting; they also provide an insight into Colquhoun’s own rapport with magic.

Eventually it becomes clear that Ménec is another Land of the Dead and that Brigid, Charlotte, and everyone there is a ghost, waiting in a limbo between bodily death and ultimate transfiguration. I Saw Water closes with a sublime sunset over the sea, in which Colquhoun’s painterly love of color, joined with her mystical Romantic tastes, carries Brigid into ecstatic communion with the elements. “There is a fluidity in Colquhoun’s work,” Mahon writes, “which echoes the flow of the sea or the wind, and which brings all the elements into harmony, usually through woman.”4

Ithell Colquhoun never gave up trying to find the combination that would unlock an emancipatory apocalypse. Like Italo Calvino, who played with a tarot pack to organize the plot of his novel The Castle of Crossed Destinies (1969), Colquhoun adopted magical structures to discern the meaning of the message from her exuberant profusion of her dream life. She was, however, acting in earnest. Whereas Breton wanted mysteries to remain mysteries and Calvino kept an ironical distance, Colquhoun had faith that everything, no matter how chaotic, ultimately has meaning and that with perseverance she would find it.
